title: PRD-5: Scale-adaptive intelligence
description:
Implement AI-driven complexity analysis that auto-adjusts Ensemble planning depth

## Problem
Ensemble requires manual complexity classification. BMAD uses scale-adaptive intelligence to auto-adjust.

## Goals
- AI analyzes work description to determine complexity
- Planning depth auto-selected based on complexity score
- Complexity score based on: scope size, dependencies, risk factors, team size

## User Stories
- As a developer, I want auto-selected planning depth so I don't manually classify work
- As a PM, I want AI complexity scoring so planning effort matches actual need

## Requirements
- FR-001: analyze-complexity command scores work description
- FR-002: Score 1-3 → Simple (fix-issue path)
- FR-003: Score 4-6 → Medium (PRD→TRD)
- FR-004: Score 7-10 → Complex (full pipeline with extra review)
- FR-005: Complexity score shown to user before planning begins
- FR-006: User can override AI classification

## Verification
- Simple bug description → score ≤3 → fix-issue path
- Complex initiative description → score ≥7 → full pipeline with extra gates
close_reason: Duplicate of br-0r3. Both specify the same routing decision -- br-iah as a 1-10 score, br-0r3 as Simple/Medium/Complex -- dispatching to the same three paths, so br-iah's FR-002/3/4 are br-0r3's bands restated and FR-006 duplicates br-0r3 FR-005. Building both would create two commands that can disagree about whether work needs a PRD, which spec section 7 forbids as a dual dispatch path. Requirements absorbed into br-0r3 (see its comments): single 'classify' command, 1-10 score shown to the user, banded for dispatch, overridable. Nothing from this bead is dropped, including its verification cases and the unresolved question of which inputs the scorer can actually read.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text: See the analysis on br-0r3. Summary: br-iah and br-0r3 specify the same routing decision at different granularities (1-10 score vs Simple/Medium/Complex bands, both dispatching to the same three paths). Implementing both yields two commands that can disagree about whether work needs a PRD, which spec section 7 forbids as a dual dispatch path. Recommend one command scoring 1-10 internally and banding for dispatch, absorbing this bead's FR-001..FR-004; FR-005/FR-006 duplicate br-0r3 FR-005. Awaiting a decision on whether to merge these two P0s before any code.

description:
## Task: TRD-016
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-b6db9749-behavior-habits-runtime.md#trd-016
PRD Reference: docs/PRD/PRD-2026-b6db9749-behavior-habits-runtime.md#req-020

--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-020**: No constitution change is ever applied without explicit human approval
No constitution change is ever applied without explicit human approval Priority: Must Reaffirms and extends the existing guarantee (`PRD-2026-15aa5acd` REQ-007) to the newly broadened evidence sources. Feature Area 7: Cross-Platform Verification

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-020-1: Given a constitution-change proposal from any evidence source | When it reaches the apply step | Then an explicit inline yes/no confirmation is required before any PR is opened
- AC-020-2: Given no confirmation is given | When evaluated | Then `constitution

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option B — dedicated adapter modules per new trigger-source type, plus a shared notification-state module.** Unchanged from 1.0.0.

New `file-source-adapter.ts` and `release-source-adapter.ts` under `packages/agent-core/src/behavior/` each produce a `BehaviorEvent` through `normalizeEvent`, mirroring the existing `pi-events.ts` → `event-translator.ts` → `normalizeEvent` → `LocalEventMatcher` chain. A new `notification-state.ts` in `pi-extension` centralises busy, duplicate and stale tracking for every behavior. Package quarantine gets its own `package-quarantine.ts` beside `package-discovery.ts`.

### Decisions added in 1.1.0

1. **How artifact changes are detected: content hashes checked at lifecycle points.** No `fs.watch`, no new dependency.
   - The adapter derives its watch set from the compiled `artifact.changed` triggers (the `path` predicate).
   - It hashes those files at `tool_result` and at `agent_end`, and emits an event when a digest differs from the last one seen in the session.
   - The hooks it relies on already exist, which is what AC-001-2 means by "supported host API".
   - It behaves the same on every OS (see REQ-023).
   - It needs no new dependency, which constitution §4 would require approval for.

   | Option | Why not chosen |
   |---|---|
   | `fs.watch` | Event semantics differ between macOS, Linux and Windows (rename-vs-change, recursive support). That is exactly the kind of per-platform behavior difference REQ-023 forbids absorbing silently. It also keeps a handle open for the whole session. |
   | `chokidar` | A new runtime dependency (constitution §4), for a problem that lifecycle-point hashing already solves. |

   The limitation, stated rather than hidden: a change is seen at the next tool call or at the end of the run, not instantly. NFR-001 measures from event validation, so this latency is outside its budget. TRD-003 reports it separately.

2. **Release signal (resolves the PRD's REQ-002 clarification): a new `v*` tag in local refs.** This matches this repo's `release.yml` (`on: push: tags: ['v*']`).
   - The tag pattern is a trigger predicate, so repositories with different conventions change configuration, not code (Rule 8).
   - It is detected two ways. First, from a successful tag-creating tool call (`git tag`, `gh release create`), in the same way `repository.changed` is derived today. Second, by diffing tag refs at session start and at `agent_end`, which covers tags that arrive by fetch.
   - It emits the **existing** catalog type `release.completed`, carrying `{ tag, sha, source }`.
   - One tag produces one event per session, whichever path sees it first.

3. **Coverage metric (resolves the PRD's REQ-016 clarification): Jest `json-summary` output, per file, `lines.pct` and `branches.pct` by default.**
   - Each package's `test:coverage` is `jest --coverage`. Jest's default reporters (`json`, `lcov`, `text`, `clover`) produce raw maps, not percentages.
   - So the behavior watches `coverage/coverage-summary.json`, and its README tells repositories to enable `json-summary`.
   - The metrics and the threshold (default 1.0 percentage point) are behavior configuration.
   - If the artifact never appears, the behavior shows up as an inert trigger in `/ensemble-status`; it is never silently idle.
   - The baseline is the previous snapshot seen **in the same session** (Rule 4). The first observation in a session only sets the baseline.

4. **The comparison is a generic command: `artifact.compare` (TRD-033).** It compares numeric JSON paths between the previous and current snapshot of an artifact and knows nothing about coverage.
   - The alternatives were rejected. Doing the comparison in an agent step would make the reported delta an unverified model claim (REQ-012). A coverage-specific command would make the third behavior need Ensemble code (REQ-018).
   - It lands in PR 1, which is why PR 5 can be configuration only.

5. **Notification transport** (REQ-009, REQ-010). `notification-state.ts` delivers to two sinks:
   - **The user**, through `SessionUiBridge.notify`, a new method that wraps `ctx.ui.notify`. Headless sessions fall back to the console.
   - **The model's context**, through `pi.sendMessage` with `display: true` and `triggerTurn: false`.

   `triggerTurn: false` is deliberate. #107 deleted the continuation path because a message that makes the agent act bypasses `MutationGuard` (`extension.ts:118-140`); a notification is data, never an instruction. Any test-derived text in a notification is fenced and labelled as data, a lesson from #94's live runs. `sendMessage` is added to `assertRequiredCapabilities`.

6. **Verified fix application** (REQ-033). This is configuration plus two small code changes.
   - A new behavior, `apply-verified-fix`, runs `mode: auto`. It triggers on `fix.verified` with the predicate `verdict: passed`, declares only `fix.apply` with no tools, and calls `fix.apply { proposalRef: ${event.payload.proposalRef} }`.
   - `CommandRegistry` then asks `ApprovalGate`. Today the prompt is only `descriptor.description` ("Apply a verified fix proposal…"), so the human would approve without seeing what changes. Code change 1 (TRD-019): the prompt names the proposal, its files and a diff summary.
   - `commit-policy.ts` has no importers today. Code change 2 (TRD-021): wire it in so an applied fix is committed with attribution.

### Alternatives considered (architecture)

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Widen the existing translator, inline notification** | Add file and release branches inside `event-translator.ts`; keep notification-state logic at each `ctx.ui.notify` call site. | `event-translator.ts` would cover three unrelated source domains. Busy/duplicate/stale logic would be copied per behavior, which is the per-reaction duplication the PRD sets out to remove. |
| **B — Dedicated adapter modules + shared notification-state module** *(chosen)* | One adapter module per source type, all feeding the same ingress; one shared notification-state module. | Matches the existing boundary (`agent-core` = provider-neutral logic, `pi-extension` = host wiring), and centralises notification state once. |
| **C — Single generic "external signal" adapter** | One configurable "watch path X for condition Y" abstraction for both sources. | Risks becoming an arbitrary-condition escape hatch around the closed, versioned catalog (REQ-CQRS-005); still duplicates notification state. |

PRD ACs: AC-020-1, AC-020-2
Target File: packages/agent-core/src/cqrs/command-registry.ts` (generic `requiresApproval` gate, regression only), packages/agent-core/src/cqrs/commands.ts` (`constitutionApply`), packages/pi-extension/src/extension.ts` (write-boundary carve-out wiring)

description:
## Test Task: TRD-009-TEST
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-f08a2a09-command-lifecycle-hooks.md#trd-009-test
PRD Reference: docs/PRD/PRD-2026-f08a2a09-command-lifecycle-hooks.md#req-022

--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-022**: Hooks from an untrusted project do not run (Must) [RISK: a cloned repository could run arbitrary executables at its first command]
Hooks from an untrusted project do not run (Must) [RISK: a cloned repository could run arbitrary executables at its first command] Goals and Non-Goals Goals: Deterministic start and end boundaries for Ensemble commands, in a harness that can honor them. A configuration contract that is validated before it can do anything. Honest reporting where a harness cannot honor a hook. Non-goals: Replacing or wrapping every harness's command execution (deferred wrapper). Observing sessions, turns or tool calls (the harnesses' own events already do). Letting a handler change what a command did. Open Questions These become the interview agenda in `/ensemble:refine-prd`. 1. Can the Pi extension host observe an aborted run? The probe below settled start and the `completed`/`error` outcomes only. An abort was not exercised; the typings declare an `aborted` outcome. A probe that aborts a running command is still needed. (REQ-004, REQ-021) 2. What is the handler output bound? The TRD sets it; the PRD requires only that a documented bound exists. (AC-009-4) Probe evidence (2026-10-15, Pi 1.2.0, `pi -p`, a throwaway extension logging events; not part of the repository): Start is observable. `input` fired with the raw slash text (`/probe-cmd hello`), then `before_agent_start` fired with the expanded template prompt, then `agent_start` and `turn_start`. The command's name and arguments are readable at `input`. A loop's end is observable, in this order: `agent_end`, then `agent_before_settle`, then `agent_settled`. Outcome is carried by `agent_before_settle`. It reported `outcome: "completed"` for a model that answered and `outcome: "error"` for three runs where the model call failed. In those error runs `agent_settled` still reported `aborted: false`, so `agent_settled` alone cannot tell success from failure. Not observed: an `aborted` outcome, `ui_prompt_start` / `ui_prompt_end`, and any event that names one command's completion. This confirms that a completion step (REQ-021) is needed, because a loop's settling says only that the loop stopped. Limits of this evidence: one `completed` run, three `error` runs with the outcome logged, three runs that produced no settle event (timeout or no response), and print mode only. The first error run predates logging of the outcome field and is not counted. Resolved in refinement (2026-10-15): A rejected invocation produces a start and an end with outcome `failed` (AC-002-2). This replaced the earlier decision that a rejected invocation produces no events: in Pi the command's own prompt validates its arguments, so the start must fire from the runtime before the workflow if it is to be deterministic and a start handler's block is to be enforced by the runtime. Found while designing the TRD (2026-10-15). For harnesses with no adapter, the guide, the capability table and a status check state that hooks are inactive; nothing is shown at command time (AC-017-2). A start handler's block produces an end event with outcome `failed` (AC-004-5). `on_error` is required on every handler (AC-010-4). The source recommendation both required explicit error behavior and defaulted end hooks to `continue`; the maintainer chose to require it. A command's end in Pi is an explicit completion step (REQ-021). Default timeouts are 5 seconds for shell handlers and 30 seconds for prompt handlers, overridable per handler (AC-009-5, AC-011-5). Selections list each command explicitly; wildcards and groups are rejected (AC-006-4). No handler runs until the project is trusted (REQ-022). A settled loop never ends a command (AC-021-4); a command that never signals completion ends as `cancelled` when the session ends or the next command begins (AC-021-5). This replaced an earlier rule that ended it as `failed` on every settle, which would have ended any command that paused to ask the user a plain-text question. Found while designing the TRD (2026-10-15). The completion instruction is carried by the adapter at run time rather than generated into every command (AC-021-1). Dependency Map REQ-001 -> none. REQ-002 depends on REQ-001. REQ-003 depends on REQ-001. REQ-004 depends on REQ-001, REQ-002. REQ-005 depends on REQ-001. REQ-006 -> none. REQ-007 depends on REQ-006. REQ-008 depends on REQ-006. REQ-009 depends on REQ-005, REQ-006, REQ-010. REQ-010 depends on REQ-006, REQ-007. REQ-011 depends on REQ-005, REQ-006, REQ-010. REQ-012 depends on REQ-009, REQ-011. REQ-013 depends on REQ-012. REQ-014 depends on REQ-001. REQ-015 depends on REQ-001 through REQ-007, REQ-009, REQ-010, REQ-012, REQ-014, REQ-021, REQ-022. REQ-016 depends on REQ-014. REQ-017 depends on REQ-014. REQ-018 depends on REQ-005, REQ-006, REQ-009, REQ-011, REQ-014. REQ-019 depends on REQ-001 through REQ-017, REQ-021, REQ-022. REQ-020 depends on REQ-009, REQ-011. REQ-021 depends on REQ-001, REQ-004, REQ-014. REQ-022 depends on REQ-006, REQ-009, REQ-017. Clusters to deliver together: Lifecycle contract: REQ-001 to REQ-005. Configuration: REQ-006 to REQ-008. Handlers: REQ-009 to REQ-013, REQ-020 and REQ-022. Adapter proof: REQ-014, REQ-015, REQ-017 and REQ-021. No circular dependencies. Implementation Readiness Gate | Dimension | Score | Note | | --- | --- | --- | | Completeness | 4 | All feature areas covered; the handler output bound is deliberately left to the TRD. | | Testability | 4 | Every Must requirement has verifiable ACs. | | Clarity | 4 | Edge cases around rejected, blocked and unfinished invocations are decided or marked, not guessed. | | Feasibility | 3 | Start, the completed/error outcomes, tool registration, the trust check and per-turn injection are confirmed in Pi. An abort is not observed, and the completion signal is still performed by the model. | Overall: 3.75 (CONCERNS), not re-scored. The 1.0.3 amendment removed a rule that could not be implemented and closed one open question, but the score was not re-evaluated, so it is left as it was. The remaining concern is Open Question 1, an abort probe. Changelog 1.0.0 (2026-10-15): Initial draft. 1.0.1 (2026-10-15): Refinement. Resolved 5 of 6 clarification items and added REQ-021 (uniform completion step) and REQ-022 (project trust). AC-005-3 made testable, AC-006-4 added, default timeouts stated. 1.0.2 (2026-10-15): Second refinement pass. Recorded Pi 1.2.0 probe evidence (start, loop end, `completed`/`error` outcome from `agent_before_settle`); narrowed Open Question 1 to the pending-question and abort cases. 1.0.3 (2026-10-15): Amended during TRD design. AC-021-1, AC-021-4 and AC-021-5 rewritten (a settle never ends a command; completion instruction carried at run time); Open Question 2 closed; clarification markers now 0. Readiness score not re-evaluated. 1.0.4 (2026-10-15): Amended during TRD design. AC-002-1, AC-002-2, AC-017-2 and AC-021-2 rewritten, AC-021-7 added: `command.start` fires at input, a rejected invocation ends as `failed`, and adapter-less harnesses are covered by documentation and a status check. Readiness score not re-evaluated.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-006-1: Given a project has `.ensemble/hooks.yaml` defining named handlers and per-command start and end selections | When a selected command runs | Then the named handlers run for the selected events
- AC-007-4: Given the configuration is invalid | When a command runs | Then no handler runs and the user sees the validation error
- AC-008-1: Given a project with no `.ensemble/hooks.yaml` | When any command runs | Then its behavior and output are identical to today's
- AC-008-2: Given a project with hooks configured only for command A | When command B runs | Then no lifecycle handler runs and no extra output appears
- AC-009-7: Given the agent's own output or tool use | When a command runs | Then no text produced by the model can start a shell handler or add one to the configuration
- AC-022-1: Given a project the host has not trusted | When a command runs | Then no handler runs, and the user sees a warning that names the hooks file and says how trust is granted
- AC-022-2: Given the project is trusted | When a command runs | Then the handlers run per the configuration
- AC-022-3: Given the active harness offers no project-trust decision | When a command runs | Then no handler runs and the user is told why
- AC-022-4: Given an untrusted project | When the hooks file is read | Then it may be validated, but nothing it names is executed

--- TRD Context ---
**Decision:** Build the lifecycle as a harness-neutral core in `packages/agent-core` (event payloads, configuration validation, redaction, a shell runner, a prompt runner, a serial dispatcher, and a per-session command-run tracker) and one adapter in `packages/pi-extension` that connects it to Pi. The adapter is the only code that knows Pi's event names.

**Decisions made by the maintainer during design (all recorded in PRD v1.0.2 to v1.0.4):**

- The first release is adapter-specific, with Pi as the proving harness. A runtime-owned wrapper is deferred.
- `command.start` fires from the runtime when the command's slash input is seen, so it never depends on the model and a start handler's block is enforced by the runtime. A command whose own prompt then rejects its arguments has already produced a start and ends as `failed`.
- A command's completion is signalled by a silent `ensemble_command_complete` tool that the model is told to call last. The instruction is injected per turn by the adapter, not generated into every Pi prompt, so projects without hooks see no change.
- A settled loop never ends a command. A command that never signals completion ends as `cancelled` when the session ends or the next command begins.
- A prompt handler is evaluated by an isolated headless child (`pi -p --no-session -ne -nt -np`), parsed against a typed response contract.
- No handler runs until the host reports the project as trusted (`ctx.isProjectTrusted()`).
- `on_error` is required on every handler. Default timeouts are 5 seconds for shell handlers and 30 seconds for prompt handlers.
- Selections list commands by name. Wildcards and groups are rejected.
- For harnesses with no adapter, the guide, a capability table and a status check say hooks are inactive. Nothing is shown at command time there.

**Why code and not a prompt (Constitution rule 8):** what runs at a command boundary, the trust check, the environment allowlist, redaction, timeouts and process cleanup are enforcement boundaries and must not be editable by a model or a user prompt. What a team wants to run (the hooks file, the executables, the prompt files) is user-owned and stays in files they edit without a toolchain.

Full title: - [ ] **TRD-015** Implement the side-effect ledger and failure record in `packages/development/lib/toolchain/ledger.js`: append each completed `sideEffect:true` call to `.ensemble/state/toolchain/ledger-<runId>.jsonl`; on adapter failure after side effects write `failure-<runId>.json` (`{adapter, capability, completedSideEffects[], error}`) with configured and well-known secret patterns redacted, also copying to `FOREMAN_ARTIFACT_PATH` when set; records are appended one line per `fs.appendFileSync` call so concurrent runs never interleave a record, `.ensemble/state/` is added to the root `.gitignore`, and the runner stops and makes no retry or resume attempt (6h)

Read-first: read the TRD, TRD Task section, PRD and PRD Requirement above before any work on this bead.


--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-014**: Mid-run failure policy (report only)
Mid-run failure policy (report only) Priority: Must If an adapter fails after side effects have occurred, the layer stops, lists every completed side effect (branches, work items, change requests), leaves state intact, and writes a machine-readable failure record. It does not retry, resume or schedule work; recovery belongs to Foreman or the user. Command and Internal-CLI Integration

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-014-1: Given an adapter failing after a branch and a work item were created | When the failure occurs | Then the command stops and its output lists both side effects
- AC-014-2: Given the same failure | When the failure record is read | Then it is machine-readable and names the adapter, failed capability and completed side effects
- AC-014-3: Given a failure | When the layer finishes | Then it has made no retry or resume attempt

--- TRD Context ---
### Alternatives Considered

| Option | Approach | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| A: Prose-only adapters | Adapter is a skill; the agent follows its prose and normalizes tool output itself | Smallest build; fully editable | Cannot route internal CLIs deterministically (REQ-016), cannot validate output (REQ-022), cannot deny at runtime (REQ-023); behavior varies per model |
| **B: Manifest plus runner (chosen)** | Adapter is a skill directory: `SKILL.md` (vocabulary and agent-facing prose) plus a declarative `adapter.yaml` (capability command templates, output mapping, allowlist, health check, detection signals, required env names). A core resolver library and `toolchain-cli` execute capabilities deterministically | Meets PRD (adapter is a skill), Rule 8 (editable without rebuild), Rule 5 (enforcement in code), REQ-016 (CLIs call the same library) | New resolver, runner, manifest schema and output-mapping engine to build and test |
| C: Executable plugin adapters | Separately packaged executables speaking a versioned JSON protocol | Arbitrary logic; strongest isolation | Contradicts the PRD's skills-as-contract decision; fails Rule 8; needs per-OS packaging and a protocol |

**Rationale:** B is the only option that makes every PRD guarantee a code-enforced property while keeping adapters user-editable data. The requester selected B at the architecture gate.

### Interpretations and Resolved Design Issues

- **I1: plain version control.** The PRD taxonomy has no plain `git` category, yet about 45 sources invoke it. Plain `git` operations (status, commit, push, log, diff, merge-base) are `vcs.*` capabilities of the `workflow` category, whose default adapter is `plain-git`; the `git-town` adapter extends it. Recommend a PRD refine pass to name this explicitly.
- **I2: ambiguity versus no signal (PRD REQ-009 AC-2 vs REQ-010 AC-2).** "No detectable signal" means no signal source exists at all (no remote, no marker files); the shipped default is used. "Ambiguous" means two or more installed adapters match, or a signal source exists (for example a remote URL) but matches no installed adapter; resolution fails explicitly in non-interactive runs and asks in interactive runs.
- **I3: AC-023-2 (governed boundary denies).** The runner is invoked through the shell tool, so a command that was not granted the shell tool cannot run any adapter; an adapter therefore cannot widen grants. The runner additionally denies any command outside the adapter's binary-plus-subcommand allowlist. Denial of raw shell commands typed by an agent outside the runner remains host-enforced (hooks on Claude Code; none in this repo for Pi, OpenCode or Codex); the lint (REQ-019) keeps commands from issuing raw tool calls. This residual is recorded in the Threat Model.
- **I4: confirmation session identity.** No stable session id is exposed uniformly across runtimes. TRD-017 begins with a spike that records which id each runtime exposes (`ENSEMBLE_SESSION_ID`, host session variables); the passive confirmation record is keyed by `(sessionKey, category, adapter, configHash)` and falls back to the run id when no session id exists.
- **I5: repo-local adapters are untrusted by default.** A cloned repository can ship `.ensemble/adapters/`. Repo-local adapters resolve in every mode (satisfying AC-007-3) but a non-interactive run additionally requires the adapter name in the user's `trustedRepoAdapters` list; an interactive run shows the adapter's allowlist at first-use confirmation.
- **I6: no new runtime dependency.** The output-mapping engine uses a small dotted-path projection (`$.a.b[0]`, `|` alternation for "array or object"), not a JSONPath library, because constitution section 4 requires approval for new dependencies.
- **I7: work-graph selection.** `work-graph` is its own category with default `auto`: use the work-graph capabilities of the resolved tracker adapter when its manifest provides them; otherwise use the built-in `work-graph-links-fallback` adapter (tracker dependency links, then plan order stated as not dependency-aware). One manifest may implement several categories.
- **I8: PRD BDD floor.** Fourteen PRD requirements (REQ-001, 002, 004, 005, 006, 009, 010, 012, 015, 018, 021, 022, 024, 025) have two ACs, below the command's three-scenario floor. The test tasks specify exactly one scenario per AC; recommend a PRD refine pass to add edge or error ACs.
- **I10: packaging.** `packages/development` depends only on `js-yaml` and its libraries require only siblings, so the resolver library, category contracts, default selection, schemas and tool inventory all ship inside `packages/development` (`lib/toolchain/` and `toolchain/`). A standalone plugin install and the Pi vendor bundle therefore contain everything; other packages call `toolchain-cli` through `TOOLCHAIN_CLI` rather than importing it.
- **I9: preflight is enforced in code.** `toolchain-cli run` refuses a side-effecting capability unless a passing preflight record exists for the supplied `--run-id`; the command prose cannot silently skip preflight.

- [ ] Given that failure, when `failure-<runId>.json` is read, then it parses as JSON and has non-empty `adapter`, `capability` and a `completedSideEffects` array of length 2; with `FOREMAN_ARTIFACT_PATH` set, an identical file exists there.

title: Adversarial phrase false-positive log
description: Feed ~50 adversarial prompts through packages/router/hooks/router.js covering every 43-phrase registry entry: negations ('do not create a PRD'), already-done ('we already created a PRD, refine it'), substring traps ('create a PRD-free zone'), mid-word collisions. comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
# br-ivv Adversarial Phrase False-Positive Log — ensemble-as-behaviors @ 71ca738+

Run 2026-09-23. 12 prompt-templates x 43 registry phrases = **516 probes** through the
real hook (`node packages/router/hooks/router.js`, stdin JSON), block-parsed for
`→ skill <name>` lines. Scripts: `scripts/adversarial-phrase-sweep.js` (raw rows →
`/tmp/ivv-raw.json`), `scripts/adversarial-phrase-report.js` (precision tables).
Reproducible: `node scripts/adversarial-phrase-sweep.js && node scripts/adversarial-phrase-report.js`.

## Result headline

- **0 unexpected skill activations.** Every firing on every probe is an exact substring
  hit on some phrase, by the documented matching contract.
- **473/473 negative-intent probes fired ≥1 skill** — 100% "false positive" by intent,
  but **462/473 are own-phrase hits** (the negation/question/trap template still contains
  the literal phrase → the owning skill surfaces). That is substring matching working
  exactly as designed; suggestion-only + "act only if it fits" framing absorbs the cost.
- **516/516 positive probes fired correctly**, 12/12 templates per phrase (perfect recall).
- **12 cross-phrase hits, one cause** — the entire precision loss of the registry in one row:

## Ambiguous phrases

| skill | phrase | defect | impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| `git-town` | `create a pr` | prefix of `create a prd` / `create a trd` (all prompts mentioning those phrases also surface git-town) | the ONLY collision: 12/516 probes |

**Recommendation for REQ-BEH-002**: add word-boundary to `create a pr`
(`" … \bcreate a pr\b"`-style — longest-match-wins, or exclude when followed by `d`/`ov`/`o`)
or drop the phrase — git-town is already covered by `create a pull request`.

## Per-phrase precision (all 43: identical shape)

Every phrase: `neg firings 11/11` (own-phrase substring, by design), `pos firings 1/1`,
`extra-skill hits` 0 except the 10 `create a pr*`-family rows. Full table:
`/tmp/ivv-report.md` (session-local; regenerate with the report script).

## False-negative companion note (from br-fnf run)

Prompts that name the artifact WITHOUT a registered verb-phrase — e.g.
"I need a PRD for the billing feature", "we should write requirements for X" — match
**zero** phrases (substring contract has no noun-only patterns). Recall gaps are in verb
phrasing coverage, not false positives. Candidates to seed: `draft the requirements`,
`spec out` (present), `requirements doc` (noun form), `PRD for`, `TRD for`.
Feeds REQ-BEH-002 alongside the collision fix.

## Method limits

- Templates cover 11 negative forms (negation x3, already-done, substring-trap, quoted-meta,
  what/why questions, past-tense, compound-neg, embedded-word) + 1 positive; no typos, no
  non-English, no multi-intent prompts.
- Registry as of 71ca738: 43 phrases / 6 skills. `glob` is a root devDependency; the sweep
  runs from the repo root.

title: Behavior outcomes are declared but never emitted, so behaviors cannot chain
description:
The workflow interpreter already computes the facts. Nothing publishes them.

EVIDENCE:
- workflow/interpreter.ts:80-82 carries 'terminal: TerminalState' and 'outcome?: string' on every run result, and line 151-154 logs { kind: 'workflow-end', behavior, terminal, outcome, reason }.
- git grep for the published types finds them ONLY in cqrs/event-authority.ts (schemas) and behavior/event-catalog.ts (the ingress list). No publish call site exists for behavior.completed, behavior.blocked, behavior.abandoned, behavior.outcome.recorded or behavior.observation.recorded.
- Meanwhile EVERY manifest declares them. .ensemble/behaviors/*/behavior.yaml all end with 'outcomes: [behavior.completed, ...]', and the compiler validates that list.

So an author declares an outcome, the compiler checks it, the interpreter reaches it, and the runtime drops it. That is a promise the runtime does not keep -- and it is invisible, because a behavior that completes looks exactly like one whose outcome went nowhere.

WHY THIS ONE FIRST, ahead of the other emission gaps: it changes what is POSSIBLE rather than what is observable. Today one behavior cannot react to another's outcome. Command-emitted events already re-enter the sink (extension.ts:304), and the comment there states the intent plainly -- 'a behavior can react to fix.verified rather than guessing from test.failure.observed'. Behavior outcomes are the missing half of that design.

SCOPE:
- Publish the interpreter's terminal result through the same sink command events use, so it reaches matcher.matchNames like everything else.
- Map terminal state to type: succeeded/inconclusive -> behavior.completed; blocked -> behavior.blocked; failed/cancelled -> behavior.abandoned. Carry the declared outcome name in the payload.
- Bounded by InvocationBudget, which already exists to make composition possible without recursion. A behavior that triggers on behavior.completed and completes must not loop -- add a test for exactly that.
- behavior.unblocked is deliberately NOT in scope: a session-scoped interpreter has no block-and-resume concept to unblock from. See the catalog bead.

TESTS: chaining works end to end; a self-triggering behavior terminates via the budget; a run that fails still emits rather than going silent.
close_reason: Fixed: workflow-dispatch publishes a behavior lifecycle event after every resolved run. succeeded/inconclusive -> behavior.completed, blocked -> behavior.blocked, failed/cancelled -> behavior.abandoned (the catalog has no behavior.failed, so the real terminal state travels in the payload). One event per run, not two -- behavior.outcome.recorded alongside would double volume to say the same thing twice. A refused stamp is logged rather than dropped, since a swallowed outcome is the defect being fixed. 5 tests including a behavior that triggers on its own completion and is stopped by InvocationBudget.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
CORRECTION 2026-09-29, after the bead was closed. The first mapping had no branch for terminal === 'inconclusive', so it fell through to behavior.completed -- publishing 'we could not tell' as 'it worked'.

That is the exact overclaim the vacuous-test-run behavior (br-cwrh) was built to catch in the same session: it uses status: inconclusive and never succeeded, precisely so a suite that executed nothing is not called a pass. Collapsing the two in the EVENT layer would have undone that distinction everywhere downstream, which is worse than never having drawn it.

Final mapping, with authorities:
  succeeded    -> behavior.completed        (observed)
  inconclusive -> behavior.outcome.recorded (diagnostic)
  blocked      -> behavior.blocked          (diagnostic)
  failed |
  cancelled    -> behavior.abandoned        (observed)

behavior.outcome.recorded carries authority 'diagnostic' rather than 'observed', which is the weaker claim wanted for a run whose result is unknown. Still one event per run.

Three tests added: inconclusive publishes outcome.recorded and explicitly NOT completed; the payload carries the real terminal state so the weaker claim is checkable; succeeded remains distinct, so the fix did not simply move the collapse somewhere else.

Also updates br-d7lm's disposition: behavior.outcome.recorded is now EMITTED, so it moves from EMIT to KEEP.

description:
## Test Task: TRD-037-TEST
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process.md#trd-037-test
PRD Reference: docs/PRD/PRD-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process.md#req-023

--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-023**: Reachable from the real entry points, on all runtimes (Must)
Reachable from the real entry points, on all runtimes (Must) New review capability is delivered through the commands people run, on every supported runtime.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-023-1: Given `fix-issue` | When it runs | Then it exercises the verified-findings, convergence and tier behavior (not just unit-tested code that nothing calls)
- AC-023-2: Given the capability is installed for Claude Code | When a review runs on each | Then the behavior is equivalent or the report states what was reduced (REQ-006)
- AC-023-3: Given the review depends on repository automation that is not configured (for example a disabled hosted reviewer) | When review runs | Then the in-agent review still runs and no new CI secret is required
- AC-024-2: Given a reviewer or verifier encounters a credential or token | When findings are reported | Then the secret value is not reproduced in any finding, comment or ledger entry

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen approach (Option C):** extend the pattern TRD-2026-82b6a138 established: **editable behavior in skills, agents and markdown; a small set of pure, deterministic libraries for what must not be self-certified by a model.**

- **User-owned (Constitution Rule 8), prose or data a maintainer edits without a toolchain:** per-area rules (`REVIEW.md` files), the policy block inside the root `REVIEW.md` (round cap, depth table, bot and maintainer logins, sensitive and High paths, Low-waiver state), severity definitions, reviewer, verifier, classifier and security-lane prompts, the PR template, the sweep and explainer procedures. All of it is read from the **target branch**, never from the PR head (REQ-024).
- **Enforcement (Rules 5 and 7), code that grades a model's claim:** vote tally, tier assignment with its sensitive-path floor and Low-waiver evidence, approval evaluation bound to a commit, the merge gate, round-cap derivation, repeat suppression, delta-range selection, depth bounds, slice coverage, metrics and eval scoring. Each is a pure CommonJS module in `packages/development/lib/`, exposed as a JSON-in/JSON-out subcommand of the existing `pr-review-cli.js`, following the 82b6a138 precedent. None performs network I/O or holds a timer.
- **Entry points (Rule 6):** every capability is reached through the one `pr-review-cycle` skill, which `fix-issue`, `implement-trd-beads` and `pr-merge` already invoke or will invoke (a new `MODE=gate` for `pr-merge`). YAML callers reference the skill only, never the CLI, as the existing parity tests require.
- **Recurrence (Rule 4):** nightly or weekly sweeps and daily eval runs are on-demand skills; a workflow template for the host repository is opt-in and scaffolded by init-project. Ensemble's own workflows gain no `schedule` trigger.

**Alternatives considered (user chose C):**

- **Option A -- prose-only skills and agents:** fewest files and fastest to ship. Rejected: the vote threshold, the tier floor, commit-bound approvals and the round cap would be prose a model can misread or skip, so none of these gates could be shown to fail (Rule 7), and "a bot approval never counts" would be a request, not a guarantee.
- **Option B -- a new TypeScript review engine in `agent-core`:** strongest typing and one runtime. Rejected: a new build and `dist` surface and cross-package coupling for a prompt-level feature, editable criteria pulled into code (against Rule 8), and drift toward an ensemble-owned dispatcher that competes with Foreman (Rule 4).

**Rationale:** Option C is the best fit for this brownfield repo. It adds only the code that grades claims, keeps everything a maintainer or adopting team would tune in files they can edit, adds no dependency (Constitution §4) and no CI secret, vendors into Pi automatically through the existing require-closure bundler, and each gate can be mutation-proven using the harness that already exists.

**Decisions taken where the PRD left a choice** (each is editable policy, not a hidden constant):

| Decision | Value | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| Policy format | Fenced `ensemble-review-policy` JSON block in the root `REVIEW.md` (no new parser dependency) | REVIEW.md, read from the base commit |
| "Cannot vouch for" a push (AC-010-3, AC-014-2) | Commit is unvouched when its tree differs from the reviewed tree and it is not a remediation commit recorded in the review-state report, or it is a merge commit | `pr-review-scope.js`, `pr-review-approvals.js` |
| Slice threshold for large PRs (AC-018-1) | 1500 changed lines, configurable | policy block |
| Area rules vs policy keys | Policy keys are read from the **root** file only; area files carry guidance, and the more restrictive instruction wins when areas conflict (AC-001-2) | skill prose |
| First PR that introduces REVIEW.md | No base copy exists, so strict defaults apply (Low treated as Medium, cap 3, default sensitive set) | `pr-review-policy.js` |
| Verifier majority | Strict majority of the expected verifier count (2 of 3, 3 of 5) | `pr-review-votes.js` |

## References
TRD: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-8d825f54-tool-abstraction-layer.md
TRD Task: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-8d825f54-tool-abstraction-layer.md#trd-026

Read-first: read the TRD, TRD Task section, PRD and PRD Requirement above before any work on this bead.


--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-016**: Tracker swap, end to end (first alternatives: Jira Cloud and Azure Boards)
Tracker swap, end to end (first alternatives: Jira Cloud and Azure Boards) Priority: Must | `[RISK: work-graph behavior differs between trackers]` With the tracker adapter changed by configuration only, every command that creates, reads, updates or closes work items works against either alternative tracker, including the internal CLIs (`trd-cli` and siblings) that currently call the default tracker directly. Those internal CLIs route through the resolved tracker adapter. The first-release Jira adapter targets Jira Cloud only.

--- TRD Context ---
### Alternatives Considered

| Option | Approach | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| A: Prose-only adapters | Adapter is a skill; the agent follows its prose and normalizes tool output itself | Smallest build; fully editable | Cannot route internal CLIs deterministically (REQ-016), cannot validate output (REQ-022), cannot deny at runtime (REQ-023); behavior varies per model |
| **B: Manifest plus runner (chosen)** | Adapter is a skill directory: `SKILL.md` (vocabulary and agent-facing prose) plus a declarative `adapter.yaml` (capability command templates, output mapping, allowlist, health check, detection signals, required env names). A core resolver library and `toolchain-cli` execute capabilities deterministically | Meets PRD (adapter is a skill), Rule 8 (editable without rebuild), Rule 5 (enforcement in code), REQ-016 (CLIs call the same library) | New resolver, runner, manifest schema and output-mapping engine to build and test |
| C: Executable plugin adapters | Separately packaged executables speaking a versioned JSON protocol | Arbitrary logic; strongest isolation | Contradicts the PRD's skills-as-contract decision; fails Rule 8; needs per-OS packaging and a protocol |

**Rationale:** B is the only option that makes every PRD guarantee a code-enforced property while keeping adapters user-editable data. The requester selected B at the architecture gate.

### Interpretations and Resolved Design Issues

- **I1: plain version control.** The PRD taxonomy has no plain `git` category, yet about 45 sources invoke it. Plain `git` operations (status, commit, push, log, diff, merge-base) are `vcs.*` capabilities of the `workflow` category, whose default adapter is `plain-git`; the `git-town` adapter extends it. Recommend a PRD refine pass to name this explicitly.
- **I2: ambiguity versus no signal (PRD REQ-009 AC-2 vs REQ-010 AC-2).** "No detectable signal" means no signal source exists at all (no remote, no marker files); the shipped default is used. "Ambiguous" means two or more installed adapters match, or a signal source exists (for example a remote URL) but matches no installed adapter; resolution fails explicitly in non-interactive runs and asks in interactive runs.
- **I3: AC-023-2 (governed boundary denies).** The runner is invoked through the shell tool, so a command that was not granted the shell tool cannot run any adapter; an adapter therefore cannot widen grants. The runner additionally denies any command outside the adapter's binary-plus-subcommand allowlist. Denial of raw shell commands typed by an agent outside the runner remains host-enforced (hooks on Claude Code; none in this repo for Pi, OpenCode or Codex); the lint (REQ-019) keeps commands from issuing raw tool calls. This residual is recorded in the Threat Model.
- **I4: confirmation session identity.** No stable session id is exposed uniformly across runtimes. TRD-017 begins with a spike that records which id each runtime exposes (`ENSEMBLE_SESSION_ID`, host session variables); the passive confirmation record is keyed by `(sessionKey, category, adapter, configHash)` and falls back to the run id when no session id exists.
- **I5: repo-local adapters are untrusted by default.** A cloned repository can ship `.ensemble/adapters/`. Repo-local adapters resolve in every mode (satisfying AC-007-3) but a non-interactive run additionally requires the adapter name in the user's `trustedRepoAdapters` list; an interactive run shows the adapter's allowlist at first-use confirmation.
- **I6: no new runtime dependency.** The output-mapping engine uses a small dotted-path projection (`$.a.b[0]`, `|` alternation for "array or object"), not a JSONPath library, because constitution section 4 requires approval for new dependencies.
- **I7: work-graph selection.** `work-graph` is its own category with default `auto`: use the work-graph capabilities of the resolved tracker adapter when its manifest provides them; otherwise use the built-in `work-graph-links-fallback` adapter (tracker dependency links, then plan order stated as not dependency-aware). One manifest may implement several categories.
- **I8: PRD BDD floor.** Fourteen PRD requirements (REQ-001, 002, 004, 005, 006, 009, 010, 012, 015, 018, 021, 022, 024, 025) have two ACs, below the command's three-scenario floor. The test tasks specify exactly one scenario per AC; recommend a PRD refine pass to add edge or error ACs.
- **I10: packaging.** `packages/development` depends only on `js-yaml` and its libraries require only siblings, so the resolver library, category contracts, default selection, schemas and tool inventory all ship inside `packages/development` (`lib/toolchain/` and `toolchain/`). A standalone plugin install and the Pi vendor bundle therefore contain everything; other packages call `toolchain-cli` through `TOOLCHAIN_CLI` rather than importing it.
- **I9: preflight is enforced in code.** `toolchain-cli run` refuses a side-effecting capability unless a passing preflight record exists for the supplied `--run-id`; the command prose cannot silently skip preflight.
Satisfies: REQ-016

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C — single enforcement seam, additive.**

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

### Architectural note carried from grounding

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

1. `pi-events.ts` emits `runtime.tool_result` / `runtime.tool.called` / `runtime.tool.failed` / `runtime.tool.completed`, none of which appear in `HARNESS_EVENT_TYPES` (which defines `runtime.tool_call.started` / `runtime.tool_call.completed`). `normalizeEvent` does not currently reject uncatalogued types, so PRD AC-002-1's "validated against the closed catalog" would be vacuous. Addressed by TRD-001 (`[satisfies INFRA]`).
2. `behavior-loader.ts:79` calls `registry.grant(...)` unconditionally immediately before `registry.invoke(...)`, making the grant boundary a rubber stamp for behavior-governed tools (unlike the echo path, where the grant is CLI-flag-gated). Addressed by TRD-003.

title: Refuse work published from a branch behind its base (hook + CI, not a behavior)
description:
DELIVERED 2026-09-29 on feature/trd-2026-0fc1c1d0-behavior-runtime-pi-harness.

RE-SCOPED FROM THE ORIGINAL PLAN. This was filed as a behavior triggering on pull_request.proposed. That was the wrong tool, chosen because the behavior runtime had just been built, not because it fit:
- nothing emits pull_request.proposed (br-jgxo), so the trigger would never fire;
- the translator sees COMPLETED tool calls, so a behavior could only ever report after the PR existed -- it cannot block;
- behaviors are async observers with no veto.

A git hook blocks synchronously, needs no model, and costs milliseconds. A third telling of the same rule would be a liability: sources that can disagree are worse than one that cannot.

SHIPPED:
- scripts/check-branch-base.js -- one implementation. Exit 0 proceed, 1 refuse, 2 could not determine. Never 0 on doubt: 'I could not check' must not resolve to 'therefore allow' (br-dowt).
- .githooks/pre-push -- fast local feedback. npm run hooks:install. NOT enforcement: --no-verify bypasses it and it does not travel with a clone.
- .github/workflows/test.yml job branch-base -- runs on PRs with fetch-depth: 0. Staged in test.yml, which is NOT a required check, so it can be observed being right before it blocks anyone. Promote to release-gate.yml later.
- scripts/__tests__/check-branch-base.test.js -- 6 tests.

BUG CAUGHT PRE-MERGE, worth recording. The first version compared against @{u}. In a CI checkout @{u} resolves to origin/<the same branch>, so the comparison was 0 0 -- exit 0, a green check that had compared nothing. Verified by running it in a --depth 1 clone. Fixed by requiring an explicit --base in CI and failing closed (exit 2, with the fetch-depth: 0 instruction in the message) when the base ref is absent.

description:
## Test Task: TRD-002-TEST
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-b6db9749-behavior-habits-runtime.md#trd-002-test
PRD Reference: docs/PRD/PRD-2026-b6db9749-behavior-habits-runtime.md#req-002

--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-002**: Support release-based trigger sources
Support release-based trigger sources Priority: Must [NEEDS CLARIFICATION: the exact release signal (tag push, published release, version-bump commit) is not specified by this PRD; left for the TRD to resolve against whichever signal the target repo already emits] A behavior can be configured to trigger when a release occurs in the current repository.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-002-1: Given a behavior package configured with a release-based trigger | When a release occurs | Then a canonical event is created carrying the release identity as evidence
- AC-002-2: Given a release-based trigger with no release actually observed | When the dispatcher evaluates other events | Then no release-triggered behavior fires

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option B — dedicated adapter modules per new trigger-source type, plus a shared notification-state module.** Unchanged from 1.0.0.

New `file-source-adapter.ts` and `release-source-adapter.ts` under `packages/agent-core/src/behavior/` each produce a `BehaviorEvent` through `normalizeEvent`, mirroring the existing `pi-events.ts` → `event-translator.ts` → `normalizeEvent` → `LocalEventMatcher` chain. A new `notification-state.ts` in `pi-extension` centralises busy, duplicate and stale tracking for every behavior. Package quarantine gets its own `package-quarantine.ts` beside `package-discovery.ts`.

### Decisions added in 1.1.0

1. **How artifact changes are detected: content hashes checked at lifecycle points.** No `fs.watch`, no new dependency.
   - The adapter derives its watch set from the compiled `artifact.changed` triggers (the `path` predicate).
   - It hashes those files at `tool_result` and at `agent_end`, and emits an event when a digest differs from the last one seen in the session.
   - The hooks it relies on already exist, which is what AC-001-2 means by "supported host API".
   - It behaves the same on every OS (see REQ-023).
   - It needs no new dependency, which constitution §4 would require approval for.

   | Option | Why not chosen |
   |---|---|
   | `fs.watch` | Event semantics differ between macOS, Linux and Windows (rename-vs-change, recursive support). That is exactly the kind of per-platform behavior difference REQ-023 forbids absorbing silently. It also keeps a handle open for the whole session. |
   | `chokidar` | A new runtime dependency (constitution §4), for a problem that lifecycle-point hashing already solves. |

   The limitation, stated rather than hidden: a change is seen at the next tool call or at the end of the run, not instantly. NFR-001 measures from event validation, so this latency is outside its budget. TRD-003 reports it separately.

2. **Release signal (resolves the PRD's REQ-002 clarification): a new `v*` tag in local refs.** This matches this repo's `release.yml` (`on: push: tags: ['v*']`).
   - The tag pattern is a trigger predicate, so repositories with different conventions change configuration, not code (Rule 8).
   - It is detected two ways. First, from a successful tag-creating tool call (`git tag`, `gh release create`), in the same way `repository.changed` is derived today. Second, by diffing tag refs at session start and at `agent_end`, which covers tags that arrive by fetch.
   - It emits the **existing** catalog type `release.completed`, carrying `{ tag, sha, source }`.
   - One tag produces one event per session, whichever path sees it first.

3. **Coverage metric (resolves the PRD's REQ-016 clarification): Jest `json-summary` output, per file, `lines.pct` and `branches.pct` by default.**
   - Each package's `test:coverage` is `jest --coverage`. Jest's default reporters (`json`, `lcov`, `text`, `clover`) produce raw maps, not percentages.
   - So the behavior watches `coverage/coverage-summary.json`, and its README tells repositories to enable `json-summary`.
   - The metrics and the threshold (default 1.0 percentage point) are behavior configuration.
   - If the artifact never appears, the behavior shows up as an inert trigger in `/ensemble-status`; it is never silently idle.
   - The baseline is the previous snapshot seen **in the same session** (Rule 4). The first observation in a session only sets the baseline.

4. **The comparison is a generic command: `artifact.compare` (TRD-033).** It compares numeric JSON paths between the previous and current snapshot of an artifact and knows nothing about coverage.
   - The alternatives were rejected. Doing the comparison in an agent step would make the reported delta an unverified model claim (REQ-012). A coverage-specific command would make the third behavior need Ensemble code (REQ-018).
   - It lands in PR 1, which is why PR 5 can be configuration only.

5. **Notification transport** (REQ-009, REQ-010). `notification-state.ts` delivers to two sinks:
   - **The user**, through `SessionUiBridge.notify`, a new method that wraps `ctx.ui.notify`. Headless sessions fall back to the console.
   - **The model's context**, through `pi.sendMessage` with `display: true` and `triggerTurn: false`.

   `triggerTurn: false` is deliberate. #107 deleted the continuation path because a message that makes the agent act bypasses `MutationGuard` (`extension.ts:118-140`); a notification is data, never an instruction. Any test-derived text in a notification is fenced and labelled as data, a lesson from #94's live runs. `sendMessage` is added to `assertRequiredCapabilities`.

6. **Verified fix application** (REQ-033). This is configuration plus two small code changes.
   - A new behavior, `apply-verified-fix`, runs `mode: auto`. It triggers on `fix.verified` with the predicate `verdict: passed`, declares only `fix.apply` with no tools, and calls `fix.apply { proposalRef: ${event.payload.proposalRef} }`.
   - `CommandRegistry` then asks `ApprovalGate`. Today the prompt is only `descriptor.description` ("Apply a verified fix proposal…"), so the human would approve without seeing what changes. Code change 1 (TRD-019): the prompt names the proposal, its files and a diff summary.
   - `commit-policy.ts` has no importers today. Code change 2 (TRD-021): wire it in so an applied fix is committed with attribution.

### Alternatives considered (architecture)

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Widen the existing translator, inline notification** | Add file and release branches inside `event-translator.ts`; keep notification-state logic at each `ctx.ui.notify` call site. | `event-translator.ts` would cover three unrelated source domains. Busy/duplicate/stale logic would be copied per behavior, which is the per-reaction duplication the PRD sets out to remove. |
| **B — Dedicated adapter modules + shared notification-state module** *(chosen)* | One adapter module per source type, all feeding the same ingress; one shared notification-state module. | Matches the existing boundary (`agent-core` = provider-neutral logic, `pi-extension` = host wiring), and centralises notification state once. |
| **C — Single generic "external signal" adapter** | One configurable "watch path X for condition Y" abstraction for both sources. | Risks becoming an arbitrary-condition escape hatch around the closed, versioned catalog (REQ-CQRS-005); still duplicates notification state. |

Verifies: TRD-002
Satisfies: REQ-002
PRD ACs Proven: AC-002-1, AC-002-2
Proof of requirement:

Actions:

Test AC:
- [ ] Scenario: a tag created in-session becomes a release event -- Given a real git repository, When a tool result reports a successful `git tag v1.2.3`, Then one `release.completed` event carries tag `v1.2.3` and that tag's sha
- [ ] Scenario: a fetched tag is caught by the ref diff -- Given a tag `v1.2.4` created outside the session, When the ref diff runs at `agent_end`, Then one `release.completed` event carries `source: "ref-diff"`
- [ ] Scenario: one tag is one release -- Given `v1.2.3` was already reported from its tool call, When the ref diff later sees the same tag, Then no second event is produced
- [ ] Scenario: no release means nothing fires -- Given only a non-matching tag `backup-1` is created, When events are evaluated, Then no `release.completed` event exists and a release-triggered behavior records no dispatch

title: The ingress event catalog is aspirational: only test.failure.observed is ever emitted
description:
Found while scoping the best-practice behaviors (br-cwrh, br-jg0l).

behavior/event-catalog.ts lists ~45 ingress event types a behavior may trigger on: prd.*, trd.*, implementation.*, review.*, validation.*, release.*, repository.*, pull_request.*, test.passed, and more. event-translator.ts emits exactly ONE of them: test.failure.observed (line 187). The pi extension otherwise emits only runtime.* telemetry.

CONSEQUENCE: a behavior authored against any other trigger compiles, validates, loads, and then never fires. There is no error and no warning -- it simply sits there looking installed. This is the failure mode that made the old example behavior's trigger unsatisfiable (cited in TRD-2026-15aa5acd as REQ-009/010/011), reappearing as a catalog that promises far more than the translator delivers.

It bit two of the five recommended behaviors immediately: br-cwrh needs test.passed (in the catalog, emitted by nothing) and br-jg0l needs pull_request.proposed (same).

OPTIONS: (a) emit more of the catalog from the translator as real signals become detectable; (b) shrink the ingress catalog to what is actually emitted and grow it deliberately; (c) keep both but have discovery WARN when a loaded behavior's trigger has no known producer, so an inert behavior announces itself.

(c) is cheap and should happen regardless of (a)/(b) -- a behavior that can never fire should say so at load time.
close_reason: Option (c) delivered: inert triggers warn at load (trigger-producers.ts, activation inertTriggers, status 'loaded but cannot fire', 12 tests). Options (a) emit more and (b) shrink the catalog are br-d7lm, which now carries the full 54-row per-event disposition and a total-coverage acceptance criterion.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
OPTION (c) DELIVERED 2026-09-29: a behavior that cannot fire now says so at load time.

- agent-core/src/behavior/trigger-producers.ts: producibleTriggers(), triggerHasProducer(), explainInertTrigger(). The explanation names what DOES fire, so a reader is not sent back to the catalog that misled them.
- behavior-activation.ts: inert triggers are collected into BehaviorActivationResult.inertTriggers and console.warn'd. A WARNING, never a skip -- an adapter may legitimately publish a type this build does not know about, and refusing to load would turn a guess into a hard failure.
- runtime-status.ts renders them under 'loaded but cannot fire', distinct from 'skipped': these ARE installed and answer manual invocation; they just cannot fire on their own, which is the part that looks identical to working.
- 10 tests.

BUG FOUND AND FIXED DURING IMPLEMENTATION, worth recording because it is the same shape as the defect being fixed. The first version derived producers from eventTypes() in cqrs/event-authority.ts. That returns 61 entries -- the whole domain vocabulary WITH PAYLOAD SCHEMAS -- and a schema describes an event's shape, it is not evidence anything emits one. prd.created has a schema and producer: 'runtime', but nothing produces it. So triggerHasProducer() returned true for everything and the check always passed: a guard that guards nothing, shipped to detect behaviors that fire on nothing. Caught by a test asserting prd.created is inert.

Producers are now derived from what is actually emitted: two translator types, eight descriptor-declared types, and command.rejected which the registry emits directly (kept in a separate constant so the drift test comparing against the catalog's emits lists does not read it as drift forever).

The hand-maintained list is pinned by a test comparing it to createCommandCatalog()'s emits, so a new command cannot leave this check reporting a live trigger as inert.

STILL OPEN: options (a) emit more of the catalog and (b) shrink the catalog to what is emitted. This change only makes the gap visible.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
SUPERSEDED IN PART by br-d7lm, which carries the measurement (10 of 54 emitted) and the proposed disposition of all 44.

Also recorded there, and it changes this bead's framing: Ensemble has NO INBOUND EVENT PATH. Two sources reach the matcher -- Pi host events plus their translations, and command handler output re-published at extension.ts:304. No webhook, no tailer, no IPC. So the prd/trd/review/pull_request/release families are not merely unemitted; they cannot arrive at all.

Option (c) -- warn at load time -- is delivered here. Options (a) emit more and (b) shrink the catalog are now br-d7lm's.

TRD: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-24fac9e9-skills-eval-harness.md

Read-first: read the TRD, TRD Task section, PRD and PRD Requirement above before any work on this bead.


--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-013**: Every result records what it was run against (Must)
Every result records what it was run against (Must)

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-013-3: Given a finished suite | When results are stored | Then a small per-skill baseline summary is written for committing to the repository and the full run logs are kept as CI artifacts
- AC-013-4: Given a baseline summary in the repository | When a regression check runs locally or in CI | Then it compares against that committed summary

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C, extend `evals/` and put runtimes behind adapters.**

The repository already has a headless behavioral eval harness (`evals/run.js`, `evals/lib/sandbox.js`, `evals/lib/graders.js`, `.github/workflows/evals.yml`, five task-keyed scenarios, unit tests with a stub `claude`). It already provides a throwaway git sandbox, deterministic graders, a total spend cap (`--max-usd`), results files and an on-demand workflow. It lacks what the PRD is mostly about:

| PRD need | State today |
|---|---|
| Evals keyed by skill, editable as files | Scenarios are keyed by task, one `scenario.json` each |
| With-skill and no-skill arms | One arm only |
| Repeats and a reliability bar | One run per scenario |
| Scrubbed environment | `spawnSync` inherits the whole environment |
| Model, skill version, eval version, runtime in results | Only a model tag |
| Coverage per skill, result cache, replay, regression compare | None |
| Pi | None |

| Option | Summary | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| A. Extend in place | Add the above to `run.js`; Pi logic added inline | Simplest, but Claude Code and Pi logic would tangle in one file |
| B. Adopt an external eval tool | Replace the runner with a third-party tool and port graders | Needs a spike and a new-dependency approval (constitution, Approval Requirements); rework of five tested scenarios; unknown support for a no-skill arm and Pi |
| **C. Extend with runner adapters** | Keep the tested runner, sandbox and graders. Add skill-keyed eval files, arms, repeats, an env allowlist, a results schema, coverage, cache and compare, behind a small runner interface with Claude Code and Pi adapters | **Chosen.** No new dependency (Node built-ins only), builds on tested code, and the eval format stays tool-neutral so an external runner could consume it later |

The PRD's Entry criterion (tool spike, fallback to a minimal in-repo runner) resolves to the fallback: this TRD is that runner, built on the existing harness. No new dependency is introduced, so no dependency approval is needed. If the owner later wants an external tool, the eval files in `evals/skills/` are the stable input.

Decisions fixed by the PRD and carried here: deterministic checks decide verdicts; judged checks only supplement and use a different model; 5 runs per arm with 4 of 5 required; $50 per suite and 900 s per run by default; results committed as per-skill baseline summaries with full logs as CI artifacts; Claude Code and Pi; on-demand CI only; advisory regression check.

- [ ] Scenario: check reads the committed summary -- Given a committed summary and a new result, When the regression check runs, Then it compares against the committed file

description:
## Test Task: TRD-029-TEST
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix.md#trd-029-test
PRD Reference: #req-007

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C — single enforcement seam, additive.**

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

### Architectural note carried from grounding

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

It implements `work-graph.ready` and `work-graph.plan`: it calls `tracker.list` and `tracker.show` through the runner, computes ready items from `dependencies[]` links when the tracker provides them (source `tracker-links`), else returns items in plan order (source `plan-order`, `dependencyAware:false`). Implementation Readiness Gate | Dimension | Score (1-5) | |-----------|-------------| | Completeness | 4.5 | | Testability | 4.5 | | Clarity | 4.5 | | Feasibility | 4.5 | | Overall | 4.5 (PASS) | Changelog | Date | Version | Changes | |------|---------|---------| | 2026-10-15 | 1.0.0 | Initial PRD | | 2026-10-15 | 1.0.1 | Refinement: AC-002-5 (stage output accepted without a prompt) and AC-002-6 (`FOREMAN_*` contract untouched) |

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-011-1: Given the new tests | When the `--foreman` parameter is removed | Then at least one test fails
- AC-011-2: Given the front-door tests | When the first-token-only rule is broken | Then a test fails

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen approach:** a prompt-only change to two YAML command sources. No TypeScript changes.

- `packages/development/commands/new-feature.yaml` gains a boolean `foreman` parameter and one derived variable, `FOREMAN`, defined once in Entry Point Resolution Step 1 and referenced by every later step. Each step that asks the user gets a `FOREMAN == true` branch that takes a deterministic, recorded, non-interactive decision. Each step that dispatches a stage skill appends `--foreman` when `FOREMAN == true`.
- `packages/development/commands/feature.yaml` (the `/ensemble:feature` front door) recognizes `--foreman` as the first token after the keyword and forwards it.
- Generated OMP, Pi and Codex artifacts are regenerated from the repo root, never hand-edited.

**Why prompt-only (Constitution Rule 8):** how a workflow behaves when no one can answer is something a maintainer would plausibly tune (for example, switching the PR gate to park instead of auto-grant). That belongs in the command prose, not in TypeScript. `RunIndexStore` already supports everything needed: `StageOutcome.detail` carries the "granted by `--foreman` policy" record.

**Additive-only edits (found in refinement):** the existing suites (`new-feature-command.test.js`, `feature-command.test.js`, `feature-input-validation-boundary.test.js`, `feature-concurrency-passthrough.test.js`) pin exact sentences in both YAML files, for example "any remaining text is an unsupported flag or argument rejected here". So no pre-existing sentence may be reworded or removed. Foreman behavior is added as new actions or appended sentences, and the existing suites must pass unchanged. For the front door that means: a new action, placed before the validation action, removes a leading `--foreman` token and sets `FOREMAN`, so the pinned validation sentences still read "remaining text" correctly; and a new action, placed after the invocation is constructed, inserts `--foreman` right after `/ensemble:new-feature` in whatever invocation was built.

**Alternatives rejected:**
- *Env-var-only detection (no flag).* Rejected: the maintainer asked for a `--foreman` flag, and the five stage skills already key on that flag.
- *A new RunRecord field `autoGranted`.* Rejected: TypeScript and schema change for information `StageOutcome.detail` already carries.
- *Parking at the approval gates.* Rejected by the maintainer: it stalls every no-user run.

title: Governed fix.verify is refused on ext4/overlay Linux (no copy-on-write), including our own CI
description:
FOUND 2026-09-29 while landing #107. createIsolatedWorkspace provisions node_modules copy-on-write only (cp -c on APFS, cp --reflink=always on btrfs/xfs) and REFUSES otherwise. That is the deliberate br-t0so design: symlink reaches the live tree (br-bxm7), and a plain copy was judged too slow.

CONSEQUENCE: on ext4, the default Linux filesystem, and on GitHub-hosted runners (proven: 'cp --reflink=always: Operation not supported' in #107's CI log), every governed verification is refused. fix.verify cannot reach 'passed' there, so fix.apply is unreachable. The propose -> verify -> apply chain is inert for those users, as br-t0so was before its fix, and CI can only assert the refusal (c1568a6), never the clone.

OPTIONS (product decision):
(a) Accept it. Document 'governed fixes need APFS/btrfs/xfs'.
(b) Fall back to a plain copy with a size/time cap and an explicit 'slow path' notice. That is still isolated, so br-bxm7 does not return.
(c) Fall back to a fresh 'npm ci' in the workspace, using a lockfile and the offline cache.
(d) Run CI on a CoW-capable runner so the clone path is exercised.
Measure (b) and (c) on this repo's node_modules before choosing. br-t0so's 'too slow' was a judgement, not a number.

description:
## Task: TRD-011
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-4dec59b8-local-ci-pr-approval.md#trd-011
PRD Reference: docs/PRD/PRD-2026-4dec59b8-local-ci-pr-approval.md#req-013

--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-013**: Cycle-time improvement is measured, not assumed (Must)
Cycle-time improvement is measured, not assumed (Must) The reduction in PR open-to-merge time is measured against a fresh, comparable baseline cohort and reported with median and p75, and the target is not claimed met until post-change data proves it.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-013-1: Given a baseline cohort and a post-change cohort of comparable PRs | When results are reported | Then median and p75 open-to-merge time are shown for both, along with the wait attributable to hosted CI and to CodeRabbit separately
- AC-013-2: Given insufficient post-change data | When status is reported | Then the target is stated as unproven rather than met
- AC-013-3: Given the gate has not yet been enabled | When the baseline is captured | Then the baseline cohort and its median and p75 are recorded before enablement, and the numeric target and minimum post-change cohort size and duration are set from that baseline and recorded in this PRD

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen approach (Option C):** A `local-ci-gate` skill owns the editable procedure; a small set of pure-JS helpers in `packages/development/lib/` owns only what must be unforgeable; `pr-merge.yaml` invokes the skill.

- `packages/development/skills/local-ci-gate/SKILL.md` is the single reusable procedure and owns everything a maintainer would plausibly tune (Constitution Rule 8): the order of the run, the messages, the bead wording, and how failures are explained.
- Pure-JS modules in `packages/development/lib/` own only what grades a claim or protects a boundary (Rules 7 and 8's enforcement exception): run-record verification, bot-vs-human classification, bead dedupe keys, approval-set config validation, and GitHub App credential handling. They make no network calls except the one module whose purpose is to post a status.
- `packages/git/commands/pr-merge.yaml` calls the skill at its existing Merge phase. It does not restate gate logic.
- The gate runs in-session in the maintainer's own process. There is no daemon, scheduler or background sweep (Rule 4; REQ-012).

**Alternatives considered (user chose C):**

- **Option A -- prose-only:** fewest files, but head-binding, run-record verification and human/bot classification would be prose a model can misread, and tests could only assert wording. Rejected: the PRD's core property is that evidence cannot be reused across commits.
- **Option B -- TypeScript runtime in agent-core:** strongest typing, but adds a build/dist surface and pulls editable criteria toward code against Rule 8. Rejected: the one place a real client is tempting (App JWT signing) needs only Node's built-in `crypto`.

**Dependency decision (user approved):** no new dependency. The App's RS256 JWT is signed with Node `crypto`; the REST calls use `fetch`. This avoids the constitution's new-dependency approval gate and keeps the signing path small and auditable.

**Rationale:** Option C matches repository precedent (TRD-2026-82b6a138), keeps editable behavior out of TypeScript, and is the minimum code that makes the trust properties testable.
Satisfies: REQ-013
PRD ACs: AC-013-1, AC-013-2, AC-013-3
Target File: packages/development/lib/local-ci-baseline.js, packages/development/skills/local-ci-gate/BASELINE.md
Actions:

Implementation AC:
- [ ] Given a cohort window, when the baseline script runs, then it reports median and p75 open-to-merge time and, separately, the wait attributable to hosted CI and to bot review
- [ ] Given the gate is not yet enabled, when the baseline is captured, then the cohort and its figures are written to a recorded note before enablement
- [ ] Given post-change data below the agreed minimum, when status is reported, then the target is stated as unproven and never as met
- [ ] Given the baseline exists, when the target and minimum post-change cohort are decided, then they are recorded in the PRD changelog
Dependencies:
close_reason: Baseline MEASURED on this repo (last 30 PRs merged to dev, 2026-10-12..21): open-to-merge median 105.9 min / p75 683.5 min; hosted CI wait median 2.6 min (~2.5%); CodeRabbit left no review on any PR, so bot-review wait is unmeasurable here. Recorded in BASELINE.md with raw rows (baseline-cohort.json); a test recomputes every figure from the rows and fails if either the note or the data is doctored (proven both ways). Maintainer decision recorded in PRD 1.0.3 changelog: no numeric target set for this repository (per adopting repository instead); status stays unproven by design. Dev suite 93/93 under Node 22.23.3.
