title: Behavior-scoped tool grants (per-invocation enforcement) instead of session-wide union
description:
## Problem

Tool grants are declared per-behavior (`capabilities.tools` in behavior.yaml)
but enforced session-wide. Enforcement is now the UNION of all loaded
behaviors' grants (see "Current state"), which composes correctly but is
coarser than the manifest implies: a behavior that declares
`tools: [read, grep]` does not actually restrict the session to those tools
if any other loaded behavior grants more.

The architecturally correct model is per-invocation scoping: a tool call made
on behalf of behavior X is checked against X's grant only.

## Why it is not implemented

Verified against pi-coding-agent source (dist/core/extensions/runner.js and
dist/core/extensions/types.d.ts, v0.87.1):

1. `emitToolCall` iterates every registered `tool_call` handler in
   registration order and returns on the FIRST `{ block: true }`:

       async emitToolCall(event) {
         for (const { handlers } of snapshotEventHandlers(this.extensions, "tool_call")) {
           for (const handler of handlers) {
             const handlerResult = await handler(event, ctx);
             if (handlerResult) {
               result = handlerResult;
               if (result.block) return result;
             }
           }
         }
         return result;
       }

   The host then throws (cli.js): `if (Q?.block) throw Error(Q.reason || ...)`.

2. `ToolCallEventBase` carries ONLY `{ type, toolCallId }` plus `toolName` and
   `input` on its variants. There is no `invocationId`, `behaviorId`,
   `activeBehavior`, or `originBehavior` field anywhere in the extension API.
   (`invocationId` exists twice in pi-agent-core's `harness/` subsystem --
   types.d.ts and runtime/progress.d.ts -- but that is the sub-agent harness,
   not reachable from an extension's tool_call handler.)

3. More fundamentally, there is currently no fact to correlate. Tool calls
   originate from the model's own turn, not from a dispatched behavior.
   Nothing "invokes" a behavior such that a subsequent bash call belongs to
   it. So "which behavior is this call for?" is not merely unplumbed --
   it is unanswerable in the present design.

## Evidence (live)

Dogfood run in /tmp/ens-fix, both `investigate-test-failure`
(tools: read, grep, glob, bash.test, git.diff) and `fix-failing-test`
(tools: read, grep, glob, bash, edit, write) loaded. `fix-failing-test`
explicitly granted `bash` and `edit`; the first `bash` call was blocked
(runtime-log: `runtime.tool_call.started tool=bash` then
`runtime.tool_call.completed isError=True`), because
`investigate-test-failure`'s handler ran first and short-circuited.

Consequence: the agent could not run the test suite, so no
`test.failure.observed` event was ever produced and NO behavior dispatched.
Enforcement prevented the system from exercising itself.

## Current state (what was shipped instead)

`wireToolGrantEnforcement` now registers ONE handler per session (keyed by a
WeakMap on the ExtensionAPI object) and blocks only if NO loaded behavior
grants the tool. Loading a behavior can only widen the grant, never silently
narrow another's. Denial message names all loaded behaviors and the union.

Covered by 3 regression tests in packages/pi-extension/tests/behavior-loader.test.ts
("tool grants compose as a union across loaded behaviors"), mutation-tested:
reverting to per-behavior wiring fails all 3.

## What a real fix requires

Behaviors need to own an execution context before per-invocation scoping is
meaningful. Options to evaluate:

- Behavior execution runs in its own sub-session/harness invocation, where
  `invocationId` already exists, and grants are attached to that invocation.
- Extension-side tagging: the behavior's registered command / sendUserMessage
  flow marks a window as "acting for behavior X", and the tool_call handler
  consults that marker. Fragile -- the model can emit tool calls outside the
  window, and concurrent/nested behaviors break the assumption.
- Upstream change to pi-coding-agent adding behavior/invocation correlation
  to ToolCallEvent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A tool call attributable to behavior X is checked against X's
      `capabilities.tools` only.
- [ ] A behavior declaring a narrow grant genuinely restricts the tools used
      on its behalf, even when a permissive behavior is also loaded.
- [ ] Load order still does not affect outcomes.
- [ ] Non-attributable tool calls (model's own turn, no behavior dispatched)
      have a defined, documented policy -- not an accidental one.
- [ ] Mutation-tested: removing the scoping makes the new tests fail.
close_reason: Implemented in ab46c82 (scope to executing behavior, not session union) and 070274a (close at agent_end, not turn_end -- a continuation spans multiple assistant turns, reproduced). Per-CALL attribution remains impossible (ToolCallEvent carries no behavior marker); the window is temporal, which is the honest approximation. 3 mutants caught. Verified live: ungranted edit/bash blocked inside the window, unscoped user bash unaffected. Remaining sub-gap tracked as AC-018-5 on br-o355 (shell redirect via a granted shell tool).

title: [trd:trd-2026-87e64cc6-command-surface-consolidation:task:TRD-016] - [ ] **TRD-016** Wire `fix-issue` entry-point resolution and checkpointing (6h)
description:
## Task: TRD-016
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-87e64cc6-command-surface-consolidation.md#trd-016
PRD Reference: #req-019

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen approach:** Two independent axes of work, both reusing existing, shipped mechanisms rather than inventing new ones.

1. **Front door (feature + issue discoverability/delegation):** Reuse the existing native-command pattern exactly as `ensemble-prd`/`ensemble-trd`/`ensemble-issue` already implement it — `registerDispatcherCommand` (completion dropdown, verbatim forward) + a `dispatch.subcommands[]`-bearing colon-named command YAML (Dispatch phase routes the first argument token to a sibling command/flag). `ensemble-feature`'s native registration and `ensemble:feature`'s dispatcher content are new; the underlying mechanism they ride on (`dispatcher-commands.ts`) is untouched.
2. **Issue resumability (REQ-019):** Option C — shared stage-agnostic I/O primitives extracted into a new `run-index-core.ts`; the existing feature `RunIndexStore` is refactored to call into it internally with its public API, `Stage`, and `RunRecord` unchanged; a new, independent `issue-run-index.ts` thin wrapper is built on the same core with its own `IssueStage`/`IssueRunRecord`. See the companion research doc for the full alternatives comparison (Option A: duplicate, Option B: fully generic store) and why C was selected live with the user during this phase.

**Alternatives considered:** Design Option A (duplicate everything, fastest, no shared plumbing) and Design Option B (fully generic parameterized store) were both presented and rejected in favor of Option C — see [Research: Run-Index Architecture](./TRD-2026-87e64cc6-command-surface-consolidation-research.md) for the full tradeoff analysis.
Satisfies: REQ-019
PRD ACs: AC-019-2, AC-019-3, AC-019-4, AC-007-3
Target File: 
Actions:

Implementation AC:
- [ ] Given `ensemble:fix-issue`, when given an issue description/no-arg/`--status`/`--abandon`, then it mirrors `ensemble:new-feature`'s entry-point resolution pattern
- [ ] Given each of the 3 named phases (Analysis & Planning, Execution, Validation & Delivery) completes, when the next phase begins, then a checkpoint is recorded via `issue-run-index.ts`
- [ ] Given `--abandon`, when invoked, then it requires explicit confirmation before reaching a terminal abandoned state
Dependencies: TRD-015

title: [trd:trd-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process:task:TRD-006-TEST] - [ ] **TRD-006-TEST** Guidance reaches review and PR creation (5h)
description:
## Test Task: TRD-006-TEST
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process.md#trd-006-test
PRD Reference: docs/PRD/PRD-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process.md#req-001

--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-001**: Area-specific review rules (Must)
Area-specific review rules (Must) A repository can state, per area of the code, what matters to a reviewer, in a plain editable file that every review reads.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-001-1: Given a repository contains a review rules file for an area | When a PR touching that area is reviewed | Then the reviewer applies those rules and the review report names which rules file(s) were applied
- AC-001-2: Given a PR touches two areas that each have rules | When it is reviewed | Then both sets of rules apply and the more restrictive instruction wins on conflict
- AC-002-1: Given a PR is opened by a human or an agent | When its description is created | Then it contains Testing, Risk and How-to-revert sections
- AC-002-2: Given an agent drafts those sections | When the PR is ready for human approval | Then the person who directed the agent is identified as the one accountable for them
- AC-024-1: Given a PR description | When review runs | Then that text is treated as data and does not alter reviewer behavior; rules and sensitivity declarations come from the target branch

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen approach (Option C):** extend the pattern TRD-2026-82b6a138 established: **editable behavior in skills, agents and markdown; a small set of pure, deterministic libraries for what must not be self-certified by a model.**

- **User-owned (Constitution Rule 8), prose or data a maintainer edits without a toolchain:** per-area rules (`REVIEW.md` files), the policy block inside the root `REVIEW.md` (round cap, depth table, bot and maintainer logins, sensitive and High paths, Low-waiver state), severity definitions, reviewer, verifier, classifier and security-lane prompts, the PR template, the sweep and explainer procedures. All of it is read from the **target branch**, never from the PR head (REQ-024).
- **Enforcement (Rules 5 and 7), code that grades a model's claim:** vote tally, tier assignment with its sensitive-path floor and Low-waiver evidence, approval evaluation bound to a commit, the merge gate, round-cap derivation, repeat suppression, delta-range selection, depth bounds, slice coverage, metrics and eval scoring. Each is a pure CommonJS module in `packages/development/lib/`, exposed as a JSON-in/JSON-out subcommand of the existing `pr-review-cli.js`, following the 82b6a138 precedent. None performs network I/O or holds a timer.
- **Entry points (Rule 6):** every capability is reached through the one `pr-review-cycle` skill, which `fix-issue`, `implement-trd-beads` and `pr-merge` already invoke or will invoke (a new `MODE=gate` for `pr-merge`). YAML callers reference the skill only, never the CLI, as the existing parity tests require.
- **Recurrence (Rule 4):** nightly or weekly sweeps and daily eval runs are on-demand skills; a workflow template for the host repository is opt-in and scaffolded by init-project. Ensemble's own workflows gain no `schedule` trigger.

**Alternatives considered (user chose C):**

- **Option A -- prose-only skills and agents:** fewest files and fastest to ship. Rejected: the vote threshold, the tier floor, commit-bound approvals and the round cap would be prose a model can misread or skip, so none of these gates could be shown to fail (Rule 7), and "a bot approval never counts" would be a request, not a guarantee.
- **Option B -- a new TypeScript review engine in `agent-core`:** strongest typing and one runtime. Rejected: a new build and `dist` surface and cross-package coupling for a prompt-level feature, editable criteria pulled into code (against Rule 8), and drift toward an ensemble-owned dispatcher that competes with Foreman (Rule 4).

**Rationale:** Option C is the best fit for this brownfield repo. It adds only the code that grades claims, keeps everything a maintainer or adopting team would tune in files they can edit, adds no dependency (Constitution §4) and no CI secret, vendors into Pi automatically through the existing require-closure bundler, and each gate can be mutation-proven using the harness that already exists.

**Decisions taken where the PRD left a choice** (each is editable policy, not a hidden constant):

| Decision | Value | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| Policy format | Fenced `ensemble-review-policy` JSON block in the root `REVIEW.md` (no new parser dependency) | REVIEW.md, read from the base commit |
| "Cannot vouch for" a push (AC-010-3, AC-014-2) | Commit is unvouched when its tree differs from the reviewed tree and it is not a remediation commit recorded in the review-state report, or it is a merge commit | `pr-review-scope.js`, `pr-review-approvals.js` |
| Slice threshold for large PRs (AC-018-1) | 1500 changed lines, configurable | policy block |
| Area rules vs policy keys | Policy keys are read from the **root** file only; area files carry guidance, and the more restrictive instruction wins when areas conflict (AC-001-2) | skill prose |
| First PR that introduces REVIEW.md | No base copy exists, so strict defaults apply (Low treated as Medium, cap 3, default sensitive set) | `pr-review-policy.js` |
| Verifier majority | Strict majority of the expected verifier count (2 of 3, 3 of 5) | `pr-review-votes.js` |
Verifies Task: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process.md#trd-006
Verifies: TRD-006
Satisfies: REQ-001
PRD ACs Proven: AC-001-1, AC-001-2, AC-002-1, AC-002-2, AC-024-1
Proof of requirement: packages/development/tests/pr-review-guidance-scenarios.test.js (25 tests, all green) drives the REAL pr-review-cli.js subcommands (policy, rules, paths, description) over a REAL git repository built per test: a base branch carrying REVIEW.md (root, with the ensemble-review-policy block), packages/core/REVIEW.md, packages/web/REVIEW.md, .github/CODEOWNERS and .github/workflows/ci.yml, and a PR branch that rewrites the policy block in its own favour, rewrites the core area file, ADDS docs/REVIEW.md and DELETES packages/web/REVIEW.md. Guidance is resolved with the exact commands SKILL.md Step 1b documents (git merge-base, git ls-tree -r --name-only <baseSha>, git show <baseSha>:<path>, git diff --name-only). AC-001-1: applied == [REVIEW.md, packages/core/REVIEW.md] for a core-only PR, every applied name resolves at the base commit, and a docs-only PR applies the root file and carries NO_AREA_RULES_NOTE. AC-001-2: both area files apply root-first with multiArea true, and the relaxing web file never governs a core path. AC-002-1: this repo's .github/pull_request_template.md filled (human) and every body fix-issue.yaml and implement-trd-beads.yaml publish (agent) are ready per the real checker; the unfilled template names all three missing sections. AC-002-2: the agent body names the accountable human; stripped or unreadable attribution is not ready, and a non-boolean agentAuthored fails closed. title: [trd:trd-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process:task:TRD-002] - [ ] **TRD-002** Review policy loader (`pr-review-policy.js`) (6h)
description:
## Task: TRD-002
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process.md#trd-002
PRD Reference: docs/PRD/PRD-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process.md#req-001

--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-001**: Area-specific review rules (Must)
Area-specific review rules (Must) A repository can state, per area of the code, what matters to a reviewer, in a plain editable file that every review reads.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-001-3: Given a maintainer wants to change what the reviewer cares about | When they edit the rules file | Then the next review reflects the change without a code change, rebuild or release
- AC-009-2: Given no repository setting | When the cap applies | Then it is 3 rounds; a repository may configure any value from 1 to 5, and a value outside that range is ignored with a warning and the default is used
- AC-009-3: Given a repository sets a different cap in its review rules | When review runs | Then that value is used by every procedure and no procedure keeps a private number
- AC-016-2: Given a maintainer wants to redefine a mode | When they edit its definition | Then the change takes effect without a code change
- AC-024-1: Given a PR description | When review runs | Then that text is treated as data and does not alter reviewer behavior; rules and sensitivity declarations come from the target branch

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen approach (Option C):** extend the pattern TRD-2026-82b6a138 established: **editable behavior in skills, agents and markdown; a small set of pure, deterministic libraries for what must not be self-certified by a model.**

- **User-owned (Constitution Rule 8), prose or data a maintainer edits without a toolchain:** per-area rules (`REVIEW.md` files), the policy block inside the root `REVIEW.md` (round cap, depth table, bot and maintainer logins, sensitive and High paths, Low-waiver state), severity definitions, reviewer, verifier, classifier and security-lane prompts, the PR template, the sweep and explainer procedures. All of it is read from the **target branch**, never from the PR head (REQ-024).
- **Enforcement (Rules 5 and 7), code that grades a model's claim:** vote tally, tier assignment with its sensitive-path floor and Low-waiver evidence, approval evaluation bound to a commit, the merge gate, round-cap derivation, repeat suppression, delta-range selection, depth bounds, slice coverage, metrics and eval scoring. Each is a pure CommonJS module in `packages/development/lib/`, exposed as a JSON-in/JSON-out subcommand of the existing `pr-review-cli.js`, following the 82b6a138 precedent. None performs network I/O or holds a timer.
- **Entry points (Rule 6):** every capability is reached through the one `pr-review-cycle` skill, which `fix-issue`, `implement-trd-beads` and `pr-merge` already invoke or will invoke (a new `MODE=gate` for `pr-merge`). YAML callers reference the skill only, never the CLI, as the existing parity tests require.
- **Recurrence (Rule 4):** nightly or weekly sweeps and daily eval runs are on-demand skills; a workflow template for the host repository is opt-in and scaffolded by init-project. Ensemble's own workflows gain no `schedule` trigger.

**Alternatives considered (user chose C):**

- **Option A -- prose-only skills and agents:** fewest files and fastest to ship. Rejected: the vote threshold, the tier floor, commit-bound approvals and the round cap would be prose a model can misread or skip, so none of these gates could be shown to fail (Rule 7), and "a bot approval never counts" would be a request, not a guarantee.
- **Option B -- a new TypeScript review engine in `agent-core`:** strongest typing and one runtime. Rejected: a new build and `dist` surface and cross-package coupling for a prompt-level feature, editable criteria pulled into code (against Rule 8), and drift toward an ensemble-owned dispatcher that competes with Foreman (Rule 4).

**Rationale:** Option C is the best fit for this brownfield repo. It adds only the code that grades claims, keeps everything a maintainer or adopting team would tune in files they can edit, adds no dependency (Constitution §4) and no CI secret, vendors into Pi automatically through the existing require-closure bundler, and each gate can be mutation-proven using the harness that already exists.

**Decisions taken where the PRD left a choice** (each is editable policy, not a hidden constant):

| Decision | Value | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| Policy format | Fenced `ensemble-review-policy` JSON block in the root `REVIEW.md` (no new parser dependency) | REVIEW.md, read from the base commit |
| "Cannot vouch for" a push (AC-010-3, AC-014-2) | Commit is unvouched when its tree differs from the reviewed tree and it is not a remediation commit recorded in the review-state report, or it is a merge commit | `pr-review-scope.js`, `pr-review-approvals.js` |
| Slice threshold for large PRs (AC-018-1) | 1500 changed lines, configurable | policy block |
| Area rules vs policy keys | Policy keys are read from the **root** file only; area files carry guidance, and the more restrictive instruction wins when areas conflict (AC-001-2) | skill prose |
| First PR that introduces REVIEW.md | No base copy exists, so strict defaults apply (Low treated as Medium, cap 3, default sensitive set) | `pr-review-policy.js` |
| Verifier majority | Strict majority of the expected verifier count (2 of 3, 3 of 5) | `pr-review-votes.js` |
Satisfies: REQ-001
PRD ACs: AC-001-3, AC-009-2, AC-009-3, AC-016-2, AC-024-1
Target File: 
Actions:

Implementation AC:
- [ ] Given the text of a root REVIEW.md with a fenced `ensemble-review-policy` JSON block, when `loadPolicy` runs, then it returns the validated policy (round cap, depth table, bot and maintainer logins, sensitive and High paths, Low-waiver state) with every unset key filled from strict defaults
- [ ] Given a configured round cap outside 1 to 5 or not an integer, when `loadPolicy` runs, then the default of 3 is used and a warning is returned; given a valid cap, then that single value is returned for every consumer
- [ ] Given a policy whose `sourceSha` differs from the review `baseSha`, or has no source identity, when `loadPolicy` runs, then it is rejected and the strict defaults apply with reason `policy-not-from-base`
- [ ] Given an unknown key, a wrong type or a depth bound that raises Quick above one reviewer or any verifier, when `loadPolicy` runs, then the key is rejected with its name and the default applies; no key is ever executed or evaluated as code
Dependencies: TRD-001
close_reason: TRD-002 implemented: lib/pr-review-policy.js + 64 Implementation AC tests + full/lib mirror. Commit a5eb8d0.

title: Governed dispatch is killed at session end: the constitution step never completes in headless runs
description:
THE ACTUAL REASON "step 3 never fires". Not capability, not the rule
provider, not missing RCA input -- the governed run is still executing when
the session ends, and dies with it.

OBSERVED, two consecutive live runs in loop-trial with instrumentation added
at the invoker entry point:

  invocation-started: "fix-failing-test"
  invocation completions: 0

The behavior matched and the governed invoker BEGAN. It never returned. No
dispatch record, no invocation record, no constitution record -- because all
three are written only after the run resolves.

CONTRAST with the earlier control run (typo repair, ~45s): that one DID log
dispatch + invocation + constitution {"status":"none"}. Same code, same
headless mode. The difference is duration: the governed run there finished
inside the session's lifetime. When the fix provider takes longer -- the
treatment scenario ran 68-98s -- the session ends first and the run is lost.

So completion is a RACE the governed path wins only by being fast. Nothing
guarantees it.

WHY THE EXISTING GUARD DOES NOT HELP
extension.ts registers:
    pi.on("session_shutdown", async () => { await drainDispatches(); });
and drainDispatches (extension.ts:100-105) loops correctly over
trackedDispatches until empty. The logic is right. It just does not hold the
process in a headless `omp -p` run: the invocation record would exist if the
drain had actually awaited the run to settle, and it does not.

NOT YET DISTINGUISHED (do not guess, instrument it):
  (a) session_shutdown is never emitted in headless mode
  (b) it is emitted, but the host exits without awaiting the async handler
Both produce what was observed; they need different fixes. A single log line
inside the shutdown hook settles it.

CONSEQUENCES
- The constitution step -- the entire learning half of the product -- is
  silently skipped whenever the fix takes more than a short while. Which is
  most real fixes.
- The same applies to every guarantee the governed path enforces. A run that
  is killed mid-flight enforced nothing and recorded nothing.
- br-zcxb's "no RCA input" hypothesis is UNTESTED, not disproved: the
  experiment designed to test it could never reach the provider. That
  question reopens once runs complete.

RELATED
br-r3om already noted the dispatch is "un-awaited ... logs nothing until it
finishes". This is the consequence of that, measured.
br-zcxb added the records that made this visible (PR #101); without them the
run looked identical to "nothing matched".
close_reason: Fixed: workflow-dispatch now writes the DispatchRecord BEFORE entering the interpreter, carrying startedAt and an 'abandoned' marker that is cleared only when the run resolves. A run cut short by session end therefore leaves evidence it STARTED, instead of leaving nothing. renderStatusReport counts abandoned separately from failed (a failure is a result; abandonment is the absence of one) and states plainly that such results are missing, not negative. Also logs kind: invocation-started. 4 tests in pi-extension/tests/abandoned-run.test.ts driving a hanging AgentPort.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
ANSWERED. It is (b): the hook fires and the process is killed mid-drain.
Cause (a) -- "session_shutdown is never emitted in headless mode" -- is
ruled out.

MEASURED, live, with both drain edges plus a 2s heartbeat:

  18:43:18.598  invocation-started
  18:44:12.244  shutdown-hook-entered  pending=1
  18:44:14.244  shutdown-drain-tick    pending=1
                process exits (61s total, agent exit=0)

session_shutdown IS emitted. The handler runs, and correctly sees pending=1.
The drain then gets exactly ONE heartbeat -- about two seconds -- before the
process dies. Not a hang: the drain was still making its first pass.

THE HOST IS NOT THE PROBLEM, which kills the obvious fix. All three emission
sites await:
  agent-session-runtime.js:106  teardownCurrent -> await emitSessionShutdownEvent
  agent-session-runtime.js:297  dispose          -> await emitSessionShutdownEvent
  agent-session.js:2606         reload           -> await emitSessionShutdownEvent
and extensions/runner.js:716 emit() awaits every handler in series with NO
timeout. So there is no host-side await to add and no timeout to lengthen.
Something exits the process roughly two seconds after shutdown begins,
independent of the handler's promise.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX. Nothing that WAITS at shutdown can work. A governed
run averaging 45-90s cannot be squeezed into a ~2s window. Viable directions:

  1. Do not start what cannot finish. Run the governed dispatch at a point
     the host genuinely blocks on (a turn boundary), not as un-awaited work
     racing the session's end.
  2. Detached worker. extension.ts already carries the note "long-running
     autofix ultimately needs a detached worker" -- this is the evidence for
     it. Survives session exit by not living in the session.
  3. Persist and resume. Write the pending invocation to disk and complete it
     on next session start. Heaviest, but the only one that survives a crash
     or a kill as well as a clean exit.

(1) is smallest and would fix the common case. (2) is what the code already
predicted it would need.

WHY THIS SURVIVED 215 PASSING TESTS -- worth fixing alongside.
Every e2e test calls drainDispatches() MANUALLY:
  tests/behavior-window.e2e.test.ts:137
  tests/live-autofix.e2e.test.ts:114
  tests/continuation-verification.e2e.test.ts, tests/one-plus-one.e2e.test.ts
So the suite proves the drain works WHEN AWAITED, and says nothing about
whether anything awaits it in production. The governed path always completes
in tests and never completes in a real headless run. Any fix here needs a
test that does not hand-call the drain, or it will pass for the same wrong
reason.

Instrumentation committed: shutdown-hook-entered / shutdown-drain-complete,
on the branch for PR #101. The completion record is kept because its absence
is the signal. The heartbeat was removed once it had done its job.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
PARTIAL CORRECTION, and a successful drain observed.

On the integration branch (both PRs merged) a full live run COMPLETED the
governed path:

  18:47:40.323  invocation-started
  18:48:14.087  shutdown-hook-entered  pending=1
  18:48:15.820  invocation                     <- completed 1.7s into drain
  18:48:15.820  shutdown-drain-complete

So the drain is genuinely awaited and it works. The earlier claim that "the
process is killed roughly two seconds into the drain" is not supported: what
is actually established is that a governed run finishing within ~2s of
shutdown completes, and the longer runs did not.

ALSO CORRECTED: my reading of the exit path. print-mode.js (the `-p` mode)
does NOT call process.exit on the normal path. Its finally block is
  await disposeRuntime()  ->  await runtimeHost.dispose()
                          ->  await emitSessionShutdownEvent(reason "quit")
and emit() awaits every handler in series. process.exit appears only in the
SIGTERM/SIGHUP handlers (print-mode.js:38-40), which also call
killTrackedDetachedChildren() first. Searched for a shutdown grace cap
(gracePeriod / shutdownTimeout / a 2000 literal) in print-mode and
agent-session-runtime: none exists.

SO THE MECHANISM IS STILL OPEN. Everything visible says the handler should be
awaited to completion, and in a short run it is. Why a longer governed run
stops -- one heartbeat at +2.0s and then nothing -- is unexplained. Candidates
worth testing, none confirmed:
  - the fix-provider child (omp -p, 120s timeout) holding something that is
    torn down with the session, so the dispatch promise never settles and the
    drain's first allSettled never returns
  - signal delivery to the process group when the parent shell's foreground
    job ends, taking the SIGTERM path and its process.exit
  - the heartbeat interval itself being cleared with the session's timers

The practical guidance on this bead is unchanged and does not depend on which
it is: work that must survive the session should not be started un-awaited
inside it. But do not implement against "there is a 2s cap" -- that was my
inference, and this run contradicts it.

Reproduction for whoever picks this up: the short path (typo repair, governed
run ~35s, completes) vs the long path (add a second test file that fails to
LOAD so the fix turn takes longer; governed run does not complete). Both in
~/Development/Sunstone/loop-trial.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
MECHANISM FOUND. It is a bounded dispose deadline in the omp host, not
anything the extension can wait its way out of. My earlier "killed ~2s into
the drain" was right; the correction that retracted it was wrong, and the
successful run did not contradict it -- it CONFIRMED it (that drain finished
in 1.73s, inside the budget).

FORENSICS, long scenario, 500ms heartbeat inside the shutdown handler:

  0.5s tick  pending=1 handles=0 reqs=0
  1.0s tick  pending=1 handles=0 reqs=0
  1.5s tick  pending=1 handles=0 reqs=0
  2.0s process-exit code=0

No signal fired (SIGTERM/SIGHUP/SIGINT/SIGPIPE were all instrumented and
none arrived). A clean exit with code 0, at 2.0s, while an await was pending
and a live setInterval existed -- which cannot happen naturally.

I WAS READING THE WRONG PACKAGE. The source I analysed is
node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent, and its print-mode.js genuinely
has no process.exit on the normal path. But `omp` is
/Users/ldangelo/.bun/bin/omp -- a COMPILED BUN SINGLE-FILE EXECUTABLE. The
behaviour is compiled in, and that also explains handles=0/reqs=0: Bun stubs
process._getActiveHandles.

Strings from the actual binary:
  "Timed out draining post-prompt tasks during dispose"
  "Post-prompt tasks still draining at dispose deadline"
  "Timed out waiting for the active agent run to settle during dispose"
  "Active agent run still settling at dispose deadline"
  "Session dispose subsystem failed during parallel teardown"
  e.drainTimeoutMs ?? z6s          where   z6s = 5000

So dispose is BOUNDED and its subsystems tear down in parallel against a
shared deadline (5000ms default on the sibling path). Our session_shutdown
handler is one of those subsystems and gets whatever is left -- measured at
about 2s twice. When the governed run fit inside it (1.73s) it completed;
when it needed 30-60s the process exited 0 and abandoned the await.

WHAT THIS SETTLES
  - Not a missing host await. Not a missing hook. Not a hang.
  - Nothing the extension does at shutdown can fix it: the budget is a few
    seconds and a governed run is 30-90s. Raising drainTimeoutMs, even if it
    were reachable from here, would mean blocking every session exit on
    arbitrary background work -- which is exactly what the deadline is there
    to prevent. The host is right.
  - The three directions on this bead stand, and (1) and (2) are now clearly
    the only real options:
      1. run the governed dispatch where the host genuinely blocks (a turn
         boundary), so it never needs to survive shutdown
      2. detached worker -- which extension.ts already predicted it would
         need
      3. persist-and-resume remains the only one that also survives a crash

UNPINNED, and I am not going to guess it: the exact budget our handler gets.
5000ms is the constant on the "active agent run settles" path; ours empirically
gets ~2s, presumably the remainder after earlier teardown. Anyone implementing
should treat the budget as "a few seconds, not guaranteed", not as a number.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
TIGHTENING the previous comment: strike "presumably the remainder after
earlier teardown". That was a guess dressed as an explanation, and it does
not survive the evidence.

z6s = 5000 does NOT reconcile with the observed cutoff, and I should not have
let it sit next to it as though it did:
  - two long runs were cut at 2.0s -- the SAME value both times, not a
    varying remainder, which is what "whatever is left of a shared 5s budget"
    would predict
  - one short run completed at 1.73s and survived

So what is actually established is empirical and narrow:
  the handler gets about 2 seconds, consistently, and work exceeding it is
  abandoned with a clean exit(0)

What is NOT established: which constant governs it. z6s = 5000 is the default
on the "active agent run settles" path (e.drainTimeoutMs ?? z6s). It may be
unrelated to the session_shutdown emit path entirely. Candidates I did not
test: a deadline computed from an earlier point than shutdown entry, or a
different bound applying to extension handlers.

Chasing the exact constant means correlating minified identifiers across a
compiled Bun binary, and it would change nothing: all three fix directions
follow from "a couple of seconds, not guaranteed", and none needs the number.

Treat the budget as unknown-but-small. Do not code against 5000, and do not
code against 2000 either -- 2.0s is what was measured on this machine, on
this build, twice.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
EVIDENCE FOR, from run 10 (2026-09-29T09:41Z). I previously wrote this bead off as 'never the blocker' -- that was based on a run where the governed path died in 65ms for an unrelated reason (br-boam), so nothing ever reached a shutdown budget. Retracting that.

Run 10, with the br-dowt hold working:

  09:41:08.300  invocation-started  behavior=fix-failing-test
  09:41:08.324  continuation        issue='npm test'
  09:42:07.466  verification        passed, heldForApproval: ['1']
  09:42:09      approval            (operator ran /ensemble-approve 1)
  09:42:15.478  runtime.session.completed
  09:55:00.100  shutdown-hook-entered / process.exited / drain-complete
  (no 'invocation' record was ever written)

The continuation half completed: fix held, approved, applied -- src/math.js is 'a + b'. The GOVERNED invocation started and never finished. No invocation record, so no constitution step, and docs/standards/constitution.md is unchanged at 5 lines.

Compare run 9, same scenario without the hold: invocation completed 13s after session end and the constitution amendment was applied. Here 13 MINUTES passed with nothing, until the external timeout killed the process.

So the constitution step is not reliably surviving session end, and run 9 may simply have been lucky with timing.

Open question, NOT yet evidence: the hold now reverts the working tree mid-run (restoreWorkingTree) while the governed fix provider is still generating against that same tree. A candidate computed from content that no longer exists is exactly what the staleness check rejects. That interaction between br-dowt's hold and the governed path needs reproducing before anyone claims it -- the invocation record that would show it was never written, which is itself the problem this bead describes.

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
RAISED TO P0 2026-09-29. Re-assessed after the user corrected my model of the Foreman/Ensemble relationship: Foreman launches and owns the session; Ensemble runs inside it as a child. That makes session lifetime THE integration seam, not an internal detail.

Why this is the worst failure shape at that seam: dispatch, invocation and constitution records are all written only after the run resolves. So when the session ends mid-run, Foreman sees a session that terminated cleanly with an empty outbox -- which is INDISTINGUISHABLE from 'the behavior correctly matched nothing and did nothing'. A silent false negative at the boundary between the two systems, in the direction that looks like success.

Anything Foreman concludes from a run that hit this -- success rates, whether a behavior is worth dispatching, whether a fix was attempted -- is drawn from data that is missing rather than negative.

Note the earlier control run logged dispatch + invocation + constitution {status: none} because it finished inside the session lifetime, i.e. the same code path succeeds or vanishes purely on duration. Fixing this likely means writing a record at invocation START (so an abandoned run is visible as abandoned), not only on resolution.

title: [trd:trd-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process:task:TRD-024-TEST] - [ ] **TRD-024-TEST** Commit-bound human approvals (6h)
description:
## Test Task: TRD-024-TEST
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process.md#trd-024-test
PRD Reference: docs/PRD/PRD-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process.md#req-014

--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-014**: Human approval means a person, on a specific commit (Must) [RISK: weak approval semantics let unreviewed code merge]
Human approval means a person, on a specific commit (Must) [RISK: weak approval semantics let unreviewed code merge] An approval is a person's decision about one commit, and an automated approval never fills a human slot.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-014-1: Given an approval is recorded by an agent or automated account | When approval requirements are evaluated | Then it does not count toward any required human approval; an account is automated if the repository's configured bot/agent list names it or the platform marks it as a bot
- AC-014-2: Given an approval was given | When new commits are pushed that the system cannot vouch for | Then the approval no longer counts and approval is requested again
- AC-014-3: Given an agent authored a PR on a person's instruction | When approvals are counted | Then that person counts as one of the required reviewers, as if they had written the code themselves
- AC-014-4: Given a High-tier PR | When approvals are counted | Then two distinct people are required
- AC-014-5: Given the Low-tier waiver has been enabled (REQ-013) | When a PR is evaluated | Then the waiver applies only to PRs authored by repository maintainers; every other author's Low PR still requires one human approval

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen approach (Option C):** extend the pattern TRD-2026-82b6a138 established: **editable behavior in skills, agents and markdown; a small set of pure, deterministic libraries for what must not be self-certified by a model.**

- **User-owned (Constitution Rule 8), prose or data a maintainer edits without a toolchain:** per-area rules (`REVIEW.md` files), the policy block inside the root `REVIEW.md` (round cap, depth table, bot and maintainer logins, sensitive and High paths, Low-waiver state), severity definitions, reviewer, verifier, classifier and security-lane prompts, the PR template, the sweep and explainer procedures. All of it is read from the **target branch**, never from the PR head (REQ-024).
- **Enforcement (Rules 5 and 7), code that grades a model's claim:** vote tally, tier assignment with its sensitive-path floor and Low-waiver evidence, approval evaluation bound to a commit, the merge gate, round-cap derivation, repeat suppression, delta-range selection, depth bounds, slice coverage, metrics and eval scoring. Each is a pure CommonJS module in `packages/development/lib/`, exposed as a JSON-in/JSON-out subcommand of the existing `pr-review-cli.js`, following the 82b6a138 precedent. None performs network I/O or holds a timer.
- **Entry points (Rule 6):** every capability is reached through the one `pr-review-cycle` skill, which `fix-issue`, `implement-trd-beads` and `pr-merge` already invoke or will invoke (a new `MODE=gate` for `pr-merge`). YAML callers reference the skill only, never the CLI, as the existing parity tests require.
- **Recurrence (Rule 4):** nightly or weekly sweeps and daily eval runs are on-demand skills; a workflow template for the host repository is opt-in and scaffolded by init-project. Ensemble's own workflows gain no `schedule` trigger.

**Alternatives considered (user chose C):**

- **Option A -- prose-only skills and agents:** fewest files and fastest to ship. Rejected: the vote threshold, the tier floor, commit-bound approvals and the round cap would be prose a model can misread or skip, so none of these gates could be shown to fail (Rule 7), and "a bot approval never counts" would be a request, not a guarantee.
- **Option B -- a new TypeScript review engine in `agent-core`:** strongest typing and one runtime. Rejected: a new build and `dist` surface and cross-package coupling for a prompt-level feature, editable criteria pulled into code (against Rule 8), and drift toward an ensemble-owned dispatcher that competes with Foreman (Rule 4).

**Rationale:** Option C is the best fit for this brownfield repo. It adds only the code that grades claims, keeps everything a maintainer or adopting team would tune in files they can edit, adds no dependency (Constitution §4) and no CI secret, vendors into Pi automatically through the existing require-closure bundler, and each gate can be mutation-proven using the harness that already exists.

**Decisions taken where the PRD left a choice** (each is editable policy, not a hidden constant):

| Decision | Value | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| Policy format | Fenced `ensemble-review-policy` JSON block in the root `REVIEW.md` (no new parser dependency) | REVIEW.md, read from the base commit |
| "Cannot vouch for" a push (AC-010-3, AC-014-2) | Commit is unvouched when its tree differs from the reviewed tree and it is not a remediation commit recorded in the review-state report, or it is a merge commit | `pr-review-scope.js`, `pr-review-approvals.js` |
| Slice threshold for large PRs (AC-018-1) | 1500 changed lines, configurable | policy block |
| Area rules vs policy keys | Policy keys are read from the **root** file only; area files carry guidance, and the more restrictive instruction wins when areas conflict (AC-001-2) | skill prose |
| First PR that introduces REVIEW.md | No base copy exists, so strict defaults apply (Low treated as Medium, cap 3, default sensitive set) | `pr-review-policy.js` |
| Verifier majority | Strict majority of the expected verifier count (2 of 3, 3 of 5) | `pr-review-votes.js` |

title: [trd:trd-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix:task:TRD-016] - [ ] **TRD-016** Guarantee non-durability: no event-to-behavior correlation is written to disk or any external store (4h)
description:
## Task: TRD-016
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-15aa5acd-live-behavior-dispatch-autofix.md#trd-016
PRD Reference: #req-003

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option C — single enforcement seam, additive.**

A new `MutationGuard` chokepoint in `agent-core` is the one place `policy.mode`, `capabilities.mutation_classes` (via the existing `hasMutationAuthority()`), and protected-path rules are resolved. It is wired once at the loader boundary rather than replicated per tool registration. The translator, matcher, and auto-fix loop are added to `pi-extension`. Discovery roots and `execution.test_command` are additive changes to existing schema/discovery code. `ToolRegistry`, `outbox`, and the compiler are reused unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — In-place extension** | Enforce mode/mutation/path rules as wrapper checks inside `behavior-loader`'s per-tool `execute()` closures. | Enforcement scattered across call sites; every future tool registration must remember to wrap. The PRD's central failure mode is *guarantees that exist in one place but are not reached from another* — Option A reproduces exactly that shape. |
| **B — Governance kernel** | Route every mutation through a `MutationBroker` + `GovernedWorkspace` in `agent-core`; `pi-extension` becomes a thin adapter. | Strongest long-term design and the right eventual target, but it re-opens already-shipped code across every tool path for a ~6-7 PR refactor before a single PRD requirement is demonstrable. Deferred deliberately, not rejected. |
| **C — Single enforcement seam** *(chosen)* | One `MutationGuard` chokepoint, wired once; everything else additive. | Gets a single auditable chokepoint (Option B's main benefit) without Option B's refactor surface. Fits the existing `agent-core` / `pi-extension` split. |

### Architectural note carried from grounding

Two defects found while grounding this design are folded into PR 1 rather than left implicit:

1. `pi-events.ts` emits `runtime.tool_result` / `runtime.tool.called` / `runtime.tool.failed` / `runtime.tool.completed`, none of which appear in `HARNESS_EVENT_TYPES` (which defines `runtime.tool_call.started` / `runtime.tool_call.completed`). `normalizeEvent` does not currently reject uncatalogued types, so PRD AC-002-1's "validated against the closed catalog" would be vacuous. Addressed by TRD-001 (`[satisfies INFRA]`).
2. `behavior-loader.ts:79` calls `registry.grant(...)` unconditionally immediately before `registry.invoke(...)`, making the grant boundary a rubber stamp for behavior-governed tools (unlike the echo path, where the grant is CLI-flag-gated). Addressed by TRD-003.
Satisfies: REQ-003
PRD ACs: AC-003-3, AC-003-4
Target File: packages/pi-extension/src/local-event-matcher.ts
Actions:

Implementation AC:
- [ ] Given a completed match-and-invoke cycle, when the process exits, then no correlation record is recoverable from disk.
Dependencies: TRD-015

title: Workflow manifests silently accept unknown step fields
description:
FOUND 2026-09-29 while authoring the pre-pr-verification and workspace-integrity behaviors (br-zctt, br-c4ni).

WHAT HAPPENED. I wrote 'next: check-tests' on command steps in both manifests, believing it wired the flow. The manifests PARSED, VALIDATED and COMPILED with zero errors. There is no 'next' field anywhere in the workflow schema -- WorkflowStepBase has only id, kind, timeout and on_failure. The key was silently discarded.

WHY IT DID NOT BREAK. The interpreter advances by DECLARATION ORDER: a non-condition step falls through to the step declared after it (interpreter.ts, the order.indexOf(step.id) + 1 path), and only conditions redirect via then/otherwise. My declaration order happened to match my intended flow, so both behaviors worked. I found it only because a TypeScript test could not read '.next' off the union.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN MY TYPO. A behavior author has no way to discover that a field is ignored:
- the compiler reports nothing
- the behavior runs
- the flow may be correct by accident, as mine were twice

The failure mode is a manifest that looks explicitly wired and is actually relying on line order. Reordering steps for readability then silently rewires the workflow, with no diagnostic at any point. This is the same class of defect as the ingress catalog (br-jgxo/br-d7lm): something that reads as a contract and is not enforced.

PROPOSED FIX. Reject unknown fields on workflow steps at validation time, naming the offending key and the step. Cheap, mechanical, and it converts a silent misunderstanding into a load-time error.

WORTH CHECKING AT THE SAME TIME: whether unknown keys are also accepted at the manifest top level (trigger/policy/capabilities), where a discarded key could mean an ungranted capability reading as granted -- a materially worse outcome than a misrouted step.

WORKAROUND IN PLACE MEANWHILE: both shipped manifests now document that flow is declaration order, and pre-pr-verification-behavior.test.ts asserts the order explicitly (commands adjacent to their checks, terminal outcomes after the last condition) so a reorder fails the build.
close_reason:
FIXED. validateWorkflow now rejects any field a step kind does not declare, naming the key and listing the allowed fields. 'next: done' -- the key I wrote into two shipped manifests believing it wired the flow -- is now a validation error instead of a silent discard.

THE FIX IS AN ALLOW-LIST, AND THAT IS THE PART WORTH REVIEWING. TypeScript interfaces do not exist at run time and a manifest is parsed YAML, so the permitted fields are written out by hand in validator.ts, duplicating schema.ts. A table that falls behind the schema would reject VALID manifests -- a worse failure than the one being fixed. So tests/workflow-unknown-fields.test.ts parses schema.ts and asserts the two agree in BOTH directions, per kind: every declared field is allowed, and nothing is allowed that is not declared. Adding a step field without updating the validator now fails the build.

A CLAIM I MADE ABOUT THIS BEAD WAS WRONG, and I would rather correct it than leave it. I suggested the laxity might let an ungranted capability read as granted. It cannot. compiler.ts requires capabilities.tools and capabilities.mutation_classes to be arrays, so a misspelled capability key yields undefined and a hard validation error. Capability typos already fail closed. The damage is the one originally filed -- a manifest that looks explicitly wired while depending on declaration order -- and no more than that.

Scope: workflow steps only. Unknown keys at manifest top level are still accepted; the required-field checks make the dangerous cases fail closed, so it is a smaller problem and not folded in here.

536 agent-core tests pass, 15 new. No shipped manifest was rejected.

title: [trd:trd-2026-1d3e0dd6-new-feature-foreman-flag:task:TRD-007] - [ ] **TRD-007** Never auto-approve untrusted event payloads (`packages/development/commands/new-feature.yaml`) (1h)
description:
## Task: TRD-007
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-1d3e0dd6-new-feature-foreman-flag.md#trd-007
PRD Reference: docs/PRD/PRD-2026-1d3e0dd6-new-feature-foreman-flag.md#req-007

--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-007**: Untrusted event payloads are never auto-approved (Must) [RISK: prompt-injection surface]
Untrusted event payloads are never auto-approved (Must) [RISK: prompt-injection surface] Front door

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-007-1: Given an event-triggered start under `--foreman` | When the payload passes `validateEventPayload` | Then it is not auto-approved: no PRD work starts, no run is created, and the pending step reports that review of the event payload requires a human
- AC-007-2: Given an event-triggered start without `--foreman` | When it runs | Then the user review happens as today
- AC-007-3: Given no `event-mapping.json` | When an event arrives | Then the default-deny behavior is unchanged

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen approach:** a prompt-only change to two YAML command sources. No TypeScript changes.

- `packages/development/commands/new-feature.yaml` gains a boolean `foreman` parameter and one derived variable, `FOREMAN`, defined once in Entry Point Resolution Step 1 and referenced by every later step. Each step that asks the user gets a `FOREMAN == true` branch that takes a deterministic, recorded, non-interactive decision. Each step that dispatches a stage skill appends `--foreman` when `FOREMAN == true`.
- `packages/development/commands/feature.yaml` (the `/ensemble:feature` front door) recognizes `--foreman` as the first token after the keyword and forwards it.
- Generated OMP, Pi and Codex artifacts are regenerated from the repo root, never hand-edited.

**Why prompt-only (Constitution Rule 8):** how a workflow behaves when no one can answer is something a maintainer would plausibly tune (for example, switching the PR gate to park instead of auto-grant). That belongs in the command prose, not in TypeScript. `RunIndexStore` already supports everything needed: `StageOutcome.detail` carries the "granted by `--foreman` policy" record.

**Additive-only edits (found in refinement):** the existing suites (`new-feature-command.test.js`, `feature-command.test.js`, `feature-input-validation-boundary.test.js`, `feature-concurrency-passthrough.test.js`) pin exact sentences in both YAML files, for example "any remaining text is an unsupported flag or argument rejected here". So no pre-existing sentence may be reworded or removed. Foreman behavior is added as new actions or appended sentences, and the existing suites must pass unchanged. For the front door that means: a new action, placed before the validation action, removes a leading `--foreman` token and sets `FOREMAN`, so the pinned validation sentences still read "remaining text" correctly; and a new action, placed after the invocation is constructed, inserts `--foreman` right after `/ensemble:new-feature` in whatever invocation was built.

**Alternatives rejected:**
- *Env-var-only detection (no flag).* Rejected: the maintainer asked for a `--foreman` flag, and the five stage skills already key on that flag.
- *A new RunRecord field `autoGranted`.* Rejected: TypeScript and schema change for information `StageOutcome.detail` already carries.
- *Parking at the approval gates.* Rejected by the maintainer: it stalls every no-user run.
Satisfies: REQ-007
PRD ACs: AC-007-1, AC-007-2, AC-007-3
Target File: 
Actions:

Implementation AC:
- [ ] Given an accepted event payload and `FOREMAN == true`, when Entry Step 5 reaches the review step, then no PRD work starts, no run is created, and the pending step reports that human review of the event payload is required
- [ ] Given `FOREMAN` is not true, when Step 5 runs, then the user review happens as today
- [ ] Given no `event-mapping.json`, when an event arrives, then default-deny is unchanged
Dependencies: TRD-006

title: [trd:trd-2026-b6db9749-behavior-habits-runtime:task:TRD-033-TEST] - [ ] **TRD-033-TEST** `artifact.compare` tests (2h)
description:
## Test Task: TRD-033-TEST
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-b6db9749-behavior-habits-runtime.md#trd-033-test
PRD Reference: docs/PRD/PRD-2026-b6db9749-behavior-habits-runtime.md#req-004

--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-004**: Adding a new behavior via an existing trigger-source type requires no Ensemble code change
Adding a new behavior via an existing trigger-source type requires no Ensemble code change Priority: Must [RISK: unresolved until at least two non-tool-call source types are actually implemented and proven config-only] A new behavior's predicate and mapping, when built on a source type that already has an adapter, are expressed entirely in the behavior package configuration; no Ensemble source file changes are needed to ship it. Feature Area 2: Read-Only Investigation Behavior Mode

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-004-1: Given a supported source type already has an adapter (built under REQ-001/REQ-002) | When a new behavior package uses that same source type with a new predicate | Then no Ensemble code changes are required to ship that behavior
- AC-016-1: Given a coverage report artifact changes (REQ-001) | When compared against the prior baseline | Then a decrease of a configured threshold or greater is detected as evidence
- AC-017-1: Given a regression is detected | When notified | Then the message states the specific coverage delta and affected file/module, not just "coverage dropped

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen: Option B — dedicated adapter modules per new trigger-source type, plus a shared notification-state module.** Unchanged from 1.0.0.

New `file-source-adapter.ts` and `release-source-adapter.ts` under `packages/agent-core/src/behavior/` each produce a `BehaviorEvent` through `normalizeEvent`, mirroring the existing `pi-events.ts` → `event-translator.ts` → `normalizeEvent` → `LocalEventMatcher` chain. A new `notification-state.ts` in `pi-extension` centralises busy, duplicate and stale tracking for every behavior. Package quarantine gets its own `package-quarantine.ts` beside `package-discovery.ts`.

### Decisions added in 1.1.0

1. **How artifact changes are detected: content hashes checked at lifecycle points.** No `fs.watch`, no new dependency.
   - The adapter derives its watch set from the compiled `artifact.changed` triggers (the `path` predicate).
   - It hashes those files at `tool_result` and at `agent_end`, and emits an event when a digest differs from the last one seen in the session.
   - The hooks it relies on already exist, which is what AC-001-2 means by "supported host API".
   - It behaves the same on every OS (see REQ-023).
   - It needs no new dependency, which constitution §4 would require approval for.

   | Option | Why not chosen |
   |---|---|
   | `fs.watch` | Event semantics differ between macOS, Linux and Windows (rename-vs-change, recursive support). That is exactly the kind of per-platform behavior difference REQ-023 forbids absorbing silently. It also keeps a handle open for the whole session. |
   | `chokidar` | A new runtime dependency (constitution §4), for a problem that lifecycle-point hashing already solves. |

   The limitation, stated rather than hidden: a change is seen at the next tool call or at the end of the run, not instantly. NFR-001 measures from event validation, so this latency is outside its budget. TRD-003 reports it separately.

2. **Release signal (resolves the PRD's REQ-002 clarification): a new `v*` tag in local refs.** This matches this repo's `release.yml` (`on: push: tags: ['v*']`).
   - The tag pattern is a trigger predicate, so repositories with different conventions change configuration, not code (Rule 8).
   - It is detected two ways. First, from a successful tag-creating tool call (`git tag`, `gh release create`), in the same way `repository.changed` is derived today. Second, by diffing tag refs at session start and at `agent_end`, which covers tags that arrive by fetch.
   - It emits the **existing** catalog type `release.completed`, carrying `{ tag, sha, source }`.
   - One tag produces one event per session, whichever path sees it first.

3. **Coverage metric (resolves the PRD's REQ-016 clarification): Jest `json-summary` output, per file, `lines.pct` and `branches.pct` by default.**
   - Each package's `test:coverage` is `jest --coverage`. Jest's default reporters (`json`, `lcov`, `text`, `clover`) produce raw maps, not percentages.
   - So the behavior watches `coverage/coverage-summary.json`, and its README tells repositories to enable `json-summary`.
   - The metrics and the threshold (default 1.0 percentage point) are behavior configuration.
   - If the artifact never appears, the behavior shows up as an inert trigger in `/ensemble-status`; it is never silently idle.
   - The baseline is the previous snapshot seen **in the same session** (Rule 4). The first observation in a session only sets the baseline.

4. **The comparison is a generic command: `artifact.compare` (TRD-033).** It compares numeric JSON paths between the previous and current snapshot of an artifact and knows nothing about coverage.
   - The alternatives were rejected. Doing the comparison in an agent step would make the reported delta an unverified model claim (REQ-012). A coverage-specific command would make the third behavior need Ensemble code (REQ-018).
   - It lands in PR 1, which is why PR 5 can be configuration only.

5. **Notification transport** (REQ-009, REQ-010). `notification-state.ts` delivers to two sinks:
   - **The user**, through `SessionUiBridge.notify`, a new method that wraps `ctx.ui.notify`. Headless sessions fall back to the console.
   - **The model's context**, through `pi.sendMessage` with `display: true` and `triggerTurn: false`.

   `triggerTurn: false` is deliberate. #107 deleted the continuation path because a message that makes the agent act bypasses `MutationGuard` (`extension.ts:118-140`); a notification is data, never an instruction. Any test-derived text in a notification is fenced and labelled as data, a lesson from #94's live runs. `sendMessage` is added to `assertRequiredCapabilities`.

6. **Verified fix application** (REQ-033). This is configuration plus two small code changes.
   - A new behavior, `apply-verified-fix`, runs `mode: auto`. It triggers on `fix.verified` with the predicate `verdict: passed`, declares only `fix.apply` with no tools, and calls `fix.apply { proposalRef: ${event.payload.proposalRef} }`.
   - `CommandRegistry` then asks `ApprovalGate`. Today the prompt is only `descriptor.description` ("Apply a verified fix proposal…"), so the human would approve without seeing what changes. Code change 1 (TRD-019): the prompt names the proposal, its files and a diff summary.
   - `commit-policy.ts` has no importers today. Code change 2 (TRD-021): wire it in so an applied fix is committed with attribution.

### Alternatives considered (architecture)

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Widen the existing translator, inline notification** | Add file and release branches inside `event-translator.ts`; keep notification-state logic at each `ctx.ui.notify` call site. | `event-translator.ts` would cover three unrelated source domains. Busy/duplicate/stale logic would be copied per behavior, which is the per-reaction duplication the PRD sets out to remove. |
| **B — Dedicated adapter modules + shared notification-state module** *(chosen)* | One adapter module per source type, all feeding the same ingress; one shared notification-state module. | Matches the existing boundary (`agent-core` = provider-neutral logic, `pi-extension` = host wiring), and centralises notification state once. |
| **C — Single generic "external signal" adapter** | One configurable "watch path X for condition Y" abstraction for both sources. | Risks becoming an arbitrary-condition escape hatch around the closed, versioned catalog (REQ-CQRS-005); still duplicates notification state. |
Verifies Task: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-b6db9749-behavior-habits-runtime.md#trd-033
Verifies: TRD-033
Satisfies: REQ-004
PRD ACs Proven: AC-004-1, AC-016-1, AC-017-1
Proof of requirement: 
Target Files: packages/agent-core/tests/artifact-compare.test.ts` (new)
Actions:

Test AC:
- [ ] Scenario: a decrease past the threshold is reported with its key and size -- Given two snapshots where `src/a.ts` `lines.pct` falls from 90 to 85 and the threshold is 1, When `artifact.compare` runs, Then it returns `{ key: "src/a.ts", metric: "lines.pct", before: 90, after: 85, delta: -5 }`
- [ ] Scenario: flat or improved metrics report nothing -- Given snapshots where every metric is equal or higher, When the command runs, Then the regression list is empty
- [ ] Scenario: a missing metric is inconclusive, never clean -- Given a snapshot lacking `branches.pct`, When the command runs, Then the verdict is `inconclusive` naming `branches.pct`
- [ ] Scenario: invalid input is rejected at the boundary -- Given `threshold: -1`, When the command is invoked, Then `CommandRegistry` rejects it on input validation before the handler runs
Dependencies: TRD-033

| Option | Summary | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Widen the existing translator, inline notification** | Add file and release branches inside `event-translator.ts`; keep notification-state logic at each `ctx.ui.notify` call site. | `event-translator.ts` would cover three unrelated source domains. Busy/duplicate/stale logic would be copied per behavior, which is the per-reaction duplication the PRD sets out to remove. |
| **B — Dedicated adapter modules + shared notification-state module** *(chosen)* | One adapter module per source type, all feeding the same ingress; one shared notification-state module. | Matches the existing boundary (`agent-core` = provider-neutral logic, `pi-extension` = host wiring), and centralises notification state once. |

**Requirement REQ-001**: `new-feature` accepts `--foreman` (Must)
`new-feature` accepts `--foreman` (Must)

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-001-1: Given `new-feature.yaml` | When its parameters are read | Then a boolean `foreman` parameter exists with default `false` and a description stating it is for automated Foreman orchestration with no user present
- AC-001-2: Given `--foreman` is absent | When any entry point or stage runs | Then every user prompt, confirmation gate and message is exactly what it is today
- AC-001-3: Given `--foreman` is present | When the invocation is parsed | Then it never changes the validation done before any run is created: `--skip-refine` and its equivalents are still rejected, and a rejected invocation creates no run

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen approach:** a prompt-only change to two YAML command sources. No TypeScript changes.

- `packages/development/commands/new-feature.yaml` gains a boolean `foreman` parameter and one derived variable, `FOREMAN`, defined once in Entry Point Resolution Step 1 and referenced by every later step. Each step that asks the user gets a `FOREMAN == true` branch that takes a deterministic, recorded, non-interactive decision. Each step that dispatches a stage skill appends `--foreman` when `FOREMAN == true`.
- `packages/development/commands/feature.yaml` (the `/ensemble:feature` front door) recognizes `--foreman` as the first token after the keyword and forwards it.
- Generated OMP, Pi and Codex artifacts are regenerated from the repo root, never hand-edited.

**Why prompt-only (Constitution Rule 8):** how a workflow behaves when no one can answer is something a maintainer would plausibly tune (for example, switching the PR gate to park instead of auto-grant). That belongs in the command prose, not in TypeScript. `RunIndexStore` already supports everything needed: `StageOutcome.detail` carries the "granted by `--foreman` policy" record.

**Additive-only edits (found in refinement):** the existing suites (`new-feature-command.test.js`, `feature-command.test.js`, `feature-input-validation-boundary.test.js`, `feature-concurrency-passthrough.test.js`) pin exact sentences in both YAML files, for example "any remaining text is an unsupported flag or argument rejected here". So no pre-existing sentence may be reworded or removed. Foreman behavior is added as new actions or appended sentences, and the existing suites must pass unchanged. For the front door that means: a new action, placed before the validation action, removes a leading `--foreman` token and sets `FOREMAN`, so the pinned validation sentences still read "remaining text" correctly; and a new action, placed after the invocation is constructed, inserts `--foreman` right after `/ensemble:new-feature` in whatever invocation was built.

**Alternatives rejected:**
- *Env-var-only detection (no flag).* Rejected: the maintainer asked for a `--foreman` flag, and the five stage skills already key on that flag.
- *A new RunRecord field `autoGranted`.* Rejected: TypeScript and schema change for information `StageOutcome.detail` already carries.
- *Parking at the approval gates.* Rejected by the maintainer: it stalls every no-user run.

PRD ACs: AC-001-1, AC-001-2, AC-001-3

title: decide which root the constitution applier should write to
description: Open design question left by PR #103 (br-x36p).
close_reason: Decided: amend the existing constitution or fail closed (resolveConstitutionPath)

comments.author: ldangelo
comments.text:
PR #103 threaded eventCwd into createConstitutionApplier(change, rootDir?) so the applier follows the repo the FAILING COMMAND ran in. That is right for the fix provider -- the patch belongs in the tree that broke. It is not obviously right for the constitution.

A constitution is a property of the PROJECT, not of whichever worktree happened to run the failing command. Writing an amendment into a throwaway worktree, a CI checkout, or a detached clone means the rule is learned and then discarded, which is the quiet failure mode: the system looks like it is governing itself while the governance evaporates.

Three candidate answers:
  1. failing command's cwd (what #103 does today)
  2. the canonical repo root -- git rev-parse --show-toplevel from the main checkout
  3. wherever the existing docs/standards/constitution.md already lives, refusing to create a second one

Option 3 is probably closest to correct: an amendment with nowhere to go should FAIL CLOSED and be reported, not silently create a new constitution in a temp directory.

Note the applier threading merged as UNTESTED plumbing -- dispatch-root.test.ts covers the fix provider and the verification suite, not the applier's root. Whatever we decide needs a test that writes from a worktree and asserts WHICH file changed.

Not urgent: the acceptance run works because the trial repo is both the failing cwd and the project root, so all three answers coincide. This only bites when they diverge.

title: [trd:trd-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process:task:TRD-028] - [ ] **TRD-028** Gate-can-fail proofs for tier floor, approval binding, security block and answered findings (5h)
description:
## Task: TRD-028
TRD Reference: docs/TRD/TRD-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process.md#trd-028
PRD Reference: docs/PRD/PRD-2026-70e784f2-code-review-process.md#req-025

--- PRD Context ---
**Requirement REQ-025**: Every new gate can fail (Must)
Every new gate can fail (Must) Each gate this work adds is shown to block a bad case. Goals and Non-Goals Goals: Reduce PR landing time by spending human attention where risk is and by presenting authors only findings that are verified. Make review converge: fewer rounds, no repeated findings, one stop rule across commands. Make human versus automated approval unambiguous and bound to a commit. Make the reviewer measurable, so improvement is demonstrated with reverts and incidents as the guardrail. Make the workflow reusable in repositories other than ensemble. Non-Goals: Replacing CodeRabbit, adding a new review provider, or editing CodeRabbit's output. Zero-human merges, or automatic tightening of approval when revert rates change. An ensemble-owned scheduler for recurring work. Enforcing a model-spend budget. Dependency Map REQ-004 depends on REQ-001, REQ-024 REQ-005 depends on REQ-004, REQ-007 REQ-006 depends on REQ-005 REQ-008 depends on REQ-006, REQ-007 REQ-010 depends on REQ-009 REQ-011 depends on REQ-007, REQ-010 REQ-012 depends on REQ-002, REQ-003 REQ-013 depends on REQ-003, REQ-012 REQ-014 depends on REQ-012 REQ-015 depends on REQ-012, REQ-013 REQ-016 depends on REQ-004, REQ-012 REQ-017 depends on REQ-005, REQ-008 REQ-018 depends on REQ-004, REQ-016 REQ-019 depends on REQ-007, REQ-009, REQ-012 REQ-020 depends on REQ-005, REQ-019 REQ-021 depends on REQ-004, REQ-016, REQ-024 REQ-022 depends on REQ-023 REQ-025 depends on REQ-005, REQ-008, REQ-009, REQ-013, REQ-014 Clusters implemented together (each independently shippable): 1. Guidance, severity and convergence: REQ-001, REQ-002, REQ-003, REQ-007, REQ-009, REQ-010, REQ-011 2. Verified findings, depth and scale: REQ-004, REQ-005, REQ-006, REQ-008, REQ-016, REQ-018 3. Risk tiers, approval semantics and the security lane: REQ-012, REQ-013, REQ-014, REQ-015, REQ-017 4. Metrics and eval set: REQ-019, REQ-020 5. Sweeps and explainers: REQ-021, REQ-022 REQ-023, REQ-024 and REQ-025 apply to every cluster. Circular dependencies: none identified. Implementation Readiness Gate | Dimension | Score (1-5) | Notes | |---|---|---| | Completeness | 4.5 | All elicited practices covered; adoption mechanism, thresholds, cohort and sweep cadence now specified | | Testability | 4 | Every Must has at least two Given/When/Then ACs and thresholds are now concrete; a few softer ACs remain (for example "delivered within minutes" in AC-022-1, "cannot vouch for" in AC-010-3 and AC-014-2) | | Clarity | 4.5 | All clarification markers resolved in 1.0.1 | | Feasibility | 4 | Within stated constraints; scope is large but split into five independently shippable clusters | | Overall | 4.25 | PASS (was 4.0) | Changelog | Date | Version | Changes | |---|---|---| | 2026-10-27 | 1.0.0 | Initial draft created via /ensemble:create-prd; Readiness Gate 4.0; Constitution Gate passed. | | 2026-10-27 | 1.0.1 | Refinement: resolved all 13 clarification markers (setup via project init flow; majority vote with 0/3/5 verifiers at Quick/Standard/Deep; cap range 1-5; kind-of-change tiers; Low waiver after 20 PRs over 30 days with zero reverts/incidents, maintainers only, no trusted list; bot list plus platform bots; default depth by tier; cohort 20 PRs and 30 days with 30/50/30% targets; code-owner-confirmed eval cases; weekly sweeps; explainers offered on High-tier PRs); Entry now requires finishing 82b6a138 first; fixed AC-013-3 ambiguity (sensitive areas are High); readiness 4.0 -> 4.25. |

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- AC-025-1: Given each of the verification threshold | When it is deliberately broken (for example a threshold set to always pass) | Then its check fails
- AC-025-2: Given a gate's check passes only in a trivial case | When it is reviewed | Then a second case that must be refused is included and refused

--- TRD Context ---
**Chosen approach (Option C):** extend the pattern TRD-2026-82b6a138 established: **editable behavior in skills, agents and markdown; a small set of pure, deterministic libraries for what must not be self-certified by a model.**

- **User-owned (Constitution Rule 8), prose or data a maintainer edits without a toolchain:** per-area rules (`REVIEW.md` files), the policy block inside the root `REVIEW.md` (round cap, depth table, bot and maintainer logins, sensitive and High paths, Low-waiver state), severity definitions, reviewer, verifier, classifier and security-lane prompts, the PR template, the sweep and explainer procedures. All of it is read from the **target branch**, never from the PR head (REQ-024).
- **Enforcement (Rules 5 and 7), code that grades a model's claim:** vote tally, tier assignment with its sensitive-path floor and Low-waiver evidence, approval evaluation bound to a commit, the merge gate, round-cap derivation, repeat suppression, delta-range selection, depth bounds, slice coverage, metrics and eval scoring. Each is a pure CommonJS module in `packages/development/lib/`, exposed as a JSON-in/JSON-out subcommand of the existing `pr-review-cli.js`, following the 82b6a138 precedent. None performs network I/O or holds a timer.
- **Entry points (Rule 6):** every capability is reached through the one `pr-review-cycle` skill, which `fix-issue`, `implement-trd-beads` and `pr-merge` already invoke or will invoke (a new `MODE=gate` for `pr-merge`). YAML callers reference the skill only, never the CLI, as the existing parity tests require.
- **Recurrence (Rule 4):** nightly or weekly sweeps and daily eval runs are on-demand skills; a workflow template for the host repository is opt-in and scaffolded by init-project. Ensemble's own workflows gain no `schedule` trigger.

**Alternatives considered (user chose C):**

- **Option A -- prose-only skills and agents:** fewest files and fastest to ship. Rejected: the vote threshold, the tier floor, commit-bound approvals and the round cap would be prose a model can misread or skip, so none of these gates could be shown to fail (Rule 7), and "a bot approval never counts" would be a request, not a guarantee.
- **Option B -- a new TypeScript review engine in `agent-core`:** strongest typing and one runtime. Rejected: a new build and `dist` surface and cross-package coupling for a prompt-level feature, editable criteria pulled into code (against Rule 8), and drift toward an ensemble-owned dispatcher that competes with Foreman (Rule 4).

**Rationale:** Option C is the best fit for this brownfield repo. It adds only the code that grades claims, keeps everything a maintainer or adopting team would tune in files they can edit, adds no dependency (Constitution §4) and no CI secret, vendors into Pi automatically through the existing require-closure bundler, and each gate can be mutation-proven using the harness that already exists.

**Decisions taken where the PRD left a choice** (each is editable policy, not a hidden constant):

| Decision | Value | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| Policy format | Fenced `ensemble-review-policy` JSON block in the root `REVIEW.md` (no new parser dependency) | REVIEW.md, read from the base commit |
| "Cannot vouch for" a push (AC-010-3, AC-014-2) | Commit is unvouched when its tree differs from the reviewed tree and it is not a remediation commit recorded in the review-state report, or it is a merge commit | `pr-review-scope.js`, `pr-review-approvals.js` |
| Slice threshold for large PRs (AC-018-1) | 1500 changed lines, configurable | policy block |
| Area rules vs policy keys | Policy keys are read from the **root** file only; area files carry guidance, and the more restrictive instruction wins when areas conflict (AC-001-2) | skill prose |
| First PR that introduces REVIEW.md | No base copy exists, so strict defaults apply (Low treated as Medium, cap 3, default sensitive set) | `pr-review-policy.js` |
| Verifier majority | Strict majority of the expected verifier count (2 of 3, 3 of 5) | `pr-review-votes.js` |

PRD ACs: AC-025-1, AC-025-2
